How to use this guide

Management is a theory-heavy subject, and that is exactly why people lose marks in it: they know the ideas but cannot write them in the way the examiner expects. This guide is organised to fix that.

Each topic is built in the same order:

  1. A simple picture (analogy): so the idea makes sense before the jargon arrives.
  2. The full explanation: everything on the slides, plus the reasoning behind it.
  3. Diagrams and tables: the exam keeps asking for “a neat diagram”, so each one is drawn here.
  4. How the exam asked it: the exact wording from past papers, with the year and question number.
  5. How to write it: the structure that earns marks.
The colour boxes

DefinitionWrite this word for word.
ExampleCorporate examples to quote.
Common confusionPairs that get mixed up.

The exam pattern (what the paper looks like)

Every endsem paper from Nov 2024 to Jun 2026 follows the same skeleton: 50 marks, 3 hours, 5 questions, each question with parts A, B, C and every part must be answered. The parts carry 3, 3 and 4 marks (sometimes 4, 3, 3). Questions are application-based: most ask you to apply or analyse, not to simply recall.

QuestionChapter it comes fromWhat usually appears
Q1 (10)Chapter 1 + start of Chapter 21A: Fayol / Mintzberg / systems approach / managerial functions and skills. 1B: CSR, ethics (three moral theories) or Japan vs USA. 1C: a case on types of plans.
Q2 (10)Chapter 2 + Chapter 32A: a strategic tool (SWOT/TOWS, BCG, Porter, Blue Ocean). 2B: organizing steps or Urwick cases. 2C: a departmentation design.
Q3 (10)Chapter 3, 4 and 53A: line / line-and-staff organisation or delegation. 3B: HRM vs HRD or job description and specification. 3C: a motivation theory case (Maslow, Herzberg or McGregor).
Q4 (10)Chapter 4 + 54A: recruitment (process or sources). 4B: training and development trends. 4C: leadership styles (authority, Likert or Managerial Grid), often a case.
Q5 (10)Chapter 4 + 55A: systems approach to staffing or induction vs orientation. 5B: communication or group development. 5C: controlling (8 steps, or types of control from a case).

The pattern behind the pattern. The same 20 or so topics keep coming back in different clothing. Systems approach to staffing has appeared in 5 of 8 papers. Line / line-and-staff in 6 of 8. Departmentation in 7 of 8. Types of control in 5 of 8. Training trends in 6 of 8. This guide gives those topics the most space.

The answer-writing playbook

Most marks in this subject are lost in presentation, not knowledge. These rules apply to every answer.

For a 3-mark part
  • Definition in one line.
  • 3 to 4 points, each with a bold heading and one explanatory line.
  • One small diagram if it is natural.
  • One real company example.
For a 4-mark part
  • Definition or framework introduction.
  • 4 to 5 points, each with a heading and 2 lines of explanation.
  • A neat labelled diagram (it is almost always worth a mark).
  • Examples, then a one-line conclusion.

“Quote the lines from the case.” This phrase appears in 8 different parts across the papers. The method is always the same:

  1. Copy the exact phrase from the case in quotation marks.
  2. Write the name of the concept it proves (for example, “Feed-forward control”).
  3. Write one line explaining why that phrase matches the concept's definition.

Do this for every concept asked. Write a table: Quoted line → Concept → Why. Examiners love this because they can tick it quickly.

“Draw a neat diagram.” Use a pencil and a scale. Label every box and arrow, give the diagram a title, and number the steps. A diagram alone is not an answer: always add 3 to 5 lines of explanation next to it.

“Apply / analyse / design for company X.” These are the 4-mark application parts. Do not give a textbook answer. Name the company, use its real products or situation in every point, and finish with an impact line (“this improves retention because…”).

Time plan (180 minutes, 5 questions). Give each question about 32 minutes, leaving 15 to 20 minutes at the end. Do not spend 20 minutes on one 3-mark part. The 10-mark question is the unit, not the 3-mark part.

Chapter 1

Basis of Management Theory and Practice

Lectures 1–8 · Business and industry · Managers and their skills · Functions · Systems approach · Fayol · Mintzberg · Environment · CSR · Ethics · Trust and change · International business

1.1 Business and industry (the starting vocabulary)

Start here: a simple picture

Think of your college canteen. The canteen itself is a business: one organisation trying to earn a profit by selling food people want. Food catering as a whole (every canteen, restaurant, caterer in the country) is an industry. A business is one player; an industry is the whole game.

Business

Definition

A business is an organisation that strives for a profit by providing goods and services desired by its customers.

  • Goods are tangible items made by businesses (a laptop, a car).
  • Services are intangible offerings that cannot be held, touched or stored (banking, a hospital visit, a cab ride).

Industry

Definition

Industry refers to economic activities that relate to the conversion of resources into useful goods. It covers production or processing of goods and materials, breeding and raising of animals, and activities in which mechanical appliances and technical skills are involved.

BasisIndustryBusiness
What it isA group of companies that produce similar goods or services; a sector of the economyAn individual company engaged in commercial activity
Characterised byThe type of product or service and the activities involvedOperates within an industry to earn profit
ExamplesAutomotive industry, technology industryTesla, Apple

Four types of industry

1
Primaryextract raw materials from the earth or sea (mining, farming, fishing, oil)
→
2
Secondaryprocess and manufacture products from raw materials (steel, cars, textiles)
→
3
Tertiaryprovide a service (banking, retail, healthcare, transport)
→
4
Quaternaryknowledge-based, high research and technology (biotechnology, computer programming)
Remember this

Primary = take it from nature. Secondary = make it. Tertiary = serve people. Quaternary = think and research. A quick test for any example: Does it extract? manufacture? serve? or research?

Why does an engineer need management?

The slides open with a small case: two people, Sneha and John, and the question “which team would you join and why?”. The point is that technical skill alone does not make a team succeed. A good engineer, within a few years, ends up leading people, handling budgets and deadlines, and talking to clients. Management gives you:

  • Planning and decision-making for projects (what to build, by when, with what resources).
  • Leading people: engineers are promoted to team leaders long before they get an MBA.
  • Cost and quality awareness: an engineering solution must also be economical.
  • Communication with non-technical clients, managers and regulators.
  • Ethical and social responsibility: engineers build things that affect society.

1.2 Managers, levels of management and managerial skills

Asked in endsemD24 · Q1AD25 · Q1A
Start here: a simple picture

Imagine a cricket team. The team owner / selection committee decides the long-term plan (which league, what squad strength). The coach turns that plan into match strategies. The captain on the field directs the players ball by ball. All three are “managers” of the same team, but each does a very different job. That is exactly what the three levels of management are.

Organisation and manager

Definition

An organisation is “a deliberate arrangement of people brought together to accomplish some specific purpose”. A manager is an individual who directs the activities of others, responsible for planning, organising, leading and controlling resources and activities to achieve specific goals.

The three levels of management

The three managerial skills

  • Technical skill: knowledge of and proficiency in a specific activity, such as a machine, a code language or accounting. (Engineer, programmer.)
  • Human (interpersonal) skill: ability to work with, understand and motivate people, as individuals and in groups. Needed equally at every level.
  • Conceptual skill: ability to see the organisation as a whole, how its parts depend on one another, and to think strategically.
LevelMain skill neededCorporate example (skill in use)
TopConceptual (+ human)A bank CEO decides to launch a digital-banking strategy for the next 5 years: sees the whole organisation and its environment.
MiddleHuman (balanced with conceptual and technical)A regional manager translates that strategy into branch targets, resolves conflict between branches, coordinates departments.
LowerTechnical (+ human)A shift supervisor on an assembly line who can fix a machine fault and guide operators on the shop floor.

Managers and administrators

The lesson plan lists “managers and administrators”. The standard distinction is: administrators (top level) decide what is to be done, framing policies and objectives; managers (middle and lower) decide how and carry out those decisions through people. In practice every top manager also does some managing, and every manager does some administering.

How the exam asked it

D25 · Q1A: “Explain the three levels of management. Examine the interrelationship between the three levels and the varying importance of managerial skills at each level. Illustrate with suitable corporate examples for each level and skill.”
D24 · Q1A: “Identify and explain the managerial functions performed by a newly joined CEO of State Bank of India. Explain which of the three managerial skills is the top priority.”

How to write it in the exam

Answer plan for D24 Q1A (SBI CEO, 4 marks): list the five functions with an SBI line each: Planning (set the bank's 5-year digital and rural-banking targets); Organizing (design branch / zonal structure, create a new digital-banking department); Staffing (appoint general managers, plan recruitment and training of officers); Leading (motivate staff, communicate vision); Controlling (monitor NPAs, profit and customer-service benchmarks). Then state that conceptual skill is the top priority for a CEO, because the job is to see the bank as a whole, read the economy and regulator (RBI), and set direction. Human skill is also essential, technical skill least.

Answer plan for D25 Q1A: three levels (with titles) → what each does → interrelationship (top sets goals, middle converts them to plans and passes information up, lower executes; problems flow upward as feedback) → skills table (above) → one corporate example per level.

1.3 The five functions of managers

Asked in endsemD24 · Q1A
Start here: a simple picture

Think of organising a college fest. First you decide what the fest will be and budget it (plan). Then you divide work into committees (organise). You pick the right students for each committee (staff). You motivate and guide them (lead). Finally you check that sales, schedule and safety are on track and fix what is going wrong (control). Management is the same loop, just with a bigger organisation.

1
Planningselect missions, objectives and the actions to achieve them; involves decision-making
→
2
Organizingestablish an intentional structure of roles for people to fill
→
3
Staffingfill and keep filled the positions in the structure
→
4
Leadinginfluence people to contribute to goals
→
5
Controllingmeasure and correct performance so events conform to plans
FunctionSlide definition (learn this)Key idea
PlanningSelecting missions and objectives as well as the actions to achieve them; it requires decision-making, which is choosing future courses of action from among alternatives.“Where are we going and how will we get there?”
OrganizingThat part of managing which involves establishing an intentional structure of roles for people to fill in an organisation. Intentional = all tasks are assigned, to the people who can do them best.Who does what, who reports to whom
StaffingFilling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure: identifying workforce requirements, inventorying people available, recruiting, selecting, placing, promoting, appraising, compensating and training.Right people in right jobs
LeadingInfluencing people so that they will contribute to organisational and group goals; the interpersonal aspect of managing. Involves motivation, leadership styles and communication.Followership: people follow those who satisfy their needs
ControllingMeasuring and correcting individual and organisational performance to ensure events conform to plans. Measures performance against goals, shows deviations, helps correct them.Plans are not self-achieving; control closes the loop
Remember this

Planning must come before controlling, because control compares actual results with plans. And communication runs through all five functions (see the systems approach, next).

1.4 Systems approach to management

Asked in endsemJ25 · Q1AJ26 · Q1A
Start here: a simple picture

A restaurant kitchen is a system. Raw ingredients, gas and chefs go in (inputs). The chefs plan, divide the work, cook and taste-check (the transformation process). Plated dishes come out (outputs). Customer reviews flow back and change tomorrow's menu (feedback). The kitchen cannot ignore what is outside: if the vegetable supplier fails or tastes change, the kitchen suffers. It is an open system: it constantly exchanges things with its environment.

The core idea

The systems approach says an organisation is a system consisting of many inter-related and inter-dependent parts (sub-systems) arranged so that the whole is more than the sum of its parts. So the parts (production, marketing, finance, HR) must be studied in their relationships, not in isolation.

Key characteristics (all from the slides)

  • Open system: depends on its external environment for inputs and is vulnerable to environmental change.
  • Inputs → transformation → outputs. Energy, information, materials and finance are drawn in, and goods and services are returned.
  • Sub-systems are mutually related: a change in one department affects others.
  • Boundary: separates what is internal from what is external, but it is permeable.
  • Every system is part of a super-system (a company belongs to an industry, which belongs to the economy).
  • Dynamic: equilibrium is always changing, so management must keep regulating and adjusting.
  • Multidisciplinary: management draws knowledge from many disciplines.
  • Communication is essential to all phases. Some outputs become inputs again.
How the exam asked it

J25 · Q1A (4): “With reference to an organization, sketch and justify how managerial functions of management and their functions work in the systems approach.”
J26 · Q1A (4): “Predict how does the ‘Systems Approach’ view an organization.”

How to write it in the exam

Start with the definition (interrelated parts, more than the sum), draw the diagram above, explain each box in one line, and justify using an example (for instance Maruti: skilled labour and steel in; planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling convert them; cars out; customer feedback fed back to design). Finish by saying why it matters: it stops managers from fixing one department while hurting another, and keeps the organisation responsive to the environment.

Common confusion

Do not confuse this with the “systems approach to staffing” in Chapter 4. That one is a separate diagram (about how staffing fits into the total management system). Both are heavily examined; they have different figures.

1.5 Fayol's 14 principles of management

Asked in endsemM25 · Q1AN25 · Q1A
Start here: a simple picture

A good football club runs on a handful of sensible rules: every player has a specialised position (division of labour), there is one coach giving instructions (unity of command), the whole team follows one game plan (unity of direction), selection is fair (equity), players are paid fairly, and the dressing room has team spirit (esprit de corps). Henri Fayol, the “Father of Modern Management Theory”, collected 14 such rules for running any organisation, at any level and in any department.

Definition

A principle is a fundamental truth that establishes a cause-and-effect relationship between two or more variables in a given situation, serving as a guide to thought and action. Management principles are statements of fundamental truth, based on logic, that guide managerial decisions and actions. They come from observation and analysis of managers' experience and from experimental studies.

Memory aid. Group the 14 into two buckets.
Bucket A, the structure of work: Division of labour · Authority and responsibility · Unity of command · Unity of direction · Order · Scalar chain · Centralisation/decentralisation.
Bucket B, how people are treated: Equity · Discipline · Initiative · Fair remuneration · Stability of tenure · Esprit de corps · Subordination of individual interest.

#PrincipleWhat it means (the line to write)Keyword that gives it away in a case
1Division of labourWork is divided and sub-divided and given to people according to their expertise; specialisation brings speed, accuracy, efficiency and economy.“assigned roles based on expertise”, “specialised tasks”
2Authority and responsibilityThey co-exist: authority is the right to get work done; responsibility is the obligation to perform. Authority without responsibility → irresponsible behaviour; responsibility without authority → ineffective person.“given power along with accountability”
3Unity of commandA subordinate receives orders from, and is accountable to, one and only one boss at a time. Avoids confusion, delay, divided loyalty, duplication.“reports to only one supervisor”
4Unity of directionOne head, one plan for a group of activities having similar objectives; all efforts directed to a common goal.“one plan”, “common goal”, “aligned with vision”
5EquityFairness, kindness and justice. Managers should be fair and impartial. Fayol allowed that at times force and harshness are needed for the sake of equity.“treated fairly”, “impartial”
6OrderProper, systematic arrangement of things (material order) and people (social order): the right person in the right job, and a place for everything.“everything in its place”, 5S, “right person right job”
7DisciplineSincerity, obedience, respect for authority and observance of rules. Needed from management too. Enforced by good superiors, clear and fair agreements, judicious penalties.“standards are clearly communicated and upheld”, penalties
8InitiativeEagerness to start action without being asked; managers should let employees suggest ideas and reward them (monetary and non-monetary).“encouraged to take ownership of ideas”, “propose improvements”
9Fair remunerationWages should be fair, reasonable and rewarding, satisfactory to both employer and employee; based on cost of living, work assigned, financial position, prevailing rates; plus benefits.“competitive salary”, “benefits”
10Stability of tenureDo not move employees too often; time is needed to learn a job, and training cost is wasted if staff leave. Stability builds team spirit.“long-term retention”, “reduce turnover”, “career development”
11Scalar chainThe chain of superiors from the ultimate authority to the lowest; all communication passes along it. A gang plank is a temporary short-cut between two points for quick communication in urgency.“chain of command”, “reporting line”
12Subordination of individual interest to general interestThe organisation is bigger than the individual, so its interest prevails; reconcile where possible, but in conflict the individual sacrifices.“put company goals above personal”
13Esprit de corpsTeam spirit: harmony and mutual understanding. Do not divide employees into competing groups; prefer face-to-face communication to written.“teamwork”, “mentorship”, “belonging”
14Centralisation and decentralisationCentralisation = decision power concentrated at the top; decentralisation = shared downward. Absolute of either is not feasible; the right balance depends on size, managers' experience, subordinates' ability.“decisions delegated to team leaders”

Unity of command vs unity of direction (a favourite comparison)

BasisUnity of commandUnity of direction
MeaningA subordinate gets orders from one bossOne head, one plan for activities with the same objective
Related toFunctioning of personnelFunctioning of departments / the organisation as a whole
Needed forFixing responsibility of each subordinateSound organisation
AdvantageAvoids conflict, confusion and chaosAvoids duplication of effort and wastage of resources
ResultBetter superior-subordinate relationshipSmooth running of the enterprise

Order and the 5S method (a slide add-on)

The slides link Order to 5S, a Japanese workplace-organisation method: Seiri (sort), Seiton (set in order / straighten), Seiso (shine / clean), Seiketsu (standardise) and Shitsuke (sustain / self-discipline). It is a practical way of achieving material order.

Centralised vs decentralised. Centralised = top-to-bottom approach (a small-town shop where the owner approves every discount). Decentralised = bottom-to-top, authority shared across levels (a chain store where each branch manager can approve local discounts). Fayol: anything that increases the subordinate's role is decentralisation; anything that decreases it is centralisation.

How the exam asked it

M25 · Q1A (4): A software firm in Udupi: “employees are assigned roles based on their expertise … expectations around deadlines and performance are clearly communicated and upheld … leadership values long-term employee retention, offering career development programs … employees are encouraged to take ownership of their ideas.” Identify and analyse Fayol's principles by citing the lines.
N25 · Q1A (4): “What are the principles of Henri Fayol? Explain any four of its importance in the system approach of management.”

Worked answer for M25 Q1A (this is exactly how to cite lines)
Line quoted from the casePrincipleWhy
“employees are assigned roles based on their expertise, ensuring that developers, designers and analysts focus on specialized tasks”Division of labourWork is divided by expertise; led to “faster project turnaround and improved software quality”.
“expectations around deadlines and performance are clearly communicated and upheld”DisciplineClear rules, observed by all, with standards enforced.
“leadership values long-term employee retention, offering career development programs and mentorship to reduce turnover”Stability of tenure (and esprit de corps via mentorship)Keeps people long enough to become productive; reduces training waste.
“employees are encouraged to take ownership of their ideas … given opportunities to lead their implementation”InitiativeStaff are allowed to originate and carry out improvements.
“maintains a professional work environment”OrderSystematic arrangement of people and work (social order).
For N25 Q1A, the 'importance in system approach' angle

Pick any four principles and link each to a system element: Division of labour → sub-systems specialise; Unity of command → clear flow of orders inside the transformation process; Unity of direction → all sub-systems pull toward the same output goal; Scalar chain → ordered communication path between sub-systems and with the environment. State that principles are flexible, not rigid; the gang plank is the proof.

1.6 Mintzberg's ten managerial roles

Asked in endsemN24 · Q1AM26 · Q1A
Start here: a simple picture

Watch a hospital head through one day: she cuts a ribbon at a new wing (a ceremonial duty), reads three emails and hears gossip about a shortage (collecting information), forwards a warning to her staff and gives a statement to the press (passing information on), then when the generator fails she handles the crisis, decides which ward gets what, and negotiates with the vendor. No single textbook “function” explains all that. Henry Mintzberg (McGill University) simply observed what managers actually do and grouped their behaviours into ten roles across three categories.

Definition

A role is an organised set of behaviours identified with a position. Mintzberg's ten roles fall into three groups: Interpersonal (dealing with people), Informational (dealing with information) and Decisional (making choices).

Each role in plain words, with the slide's example

CategoryRoleMeaningExample
InterpersonalFigureheadCeremonial and symbolic duties because of position; routine, little serious decision-making, but not to be ignored.President greets visiting dignitaries; foreman attends a worker's wedding; sales manager takes a key customer to lunch.
LeaderResponsible for the work of the unit: hiring, training, motivating, reconciling individual needs with goals.Manager motivating and encouraging her team; hiring and training staff.
LiaisonBuilding contacts outside the vertical chain of command (peers and outsiders) mostly to get information.An engineering head networking with other department heads, suppliers and industry bodies.
InformationalMonitorContinuously scans the environment for information (much of it soft: gossip, hearsay, speculation), using contacts and subordinates.Reading industry reports, listening to rumours of a supplier's problems.
DisseminatorShares and distributes information within the organisation, including privileged information, and passes information between subordinates.Briefing the team on a new client requirement learned at a meeting.
SpokespersonSends information to people outside the unit, and satisfies influential outsiders.Informing directors and shareholders of financial performance; assuring consumer groups and government of compliance.
DecisionalEntrepreneurVoluntary initiator of change; seeks to improve the unit; like a juggler keeping many development projects in the air.CEO launching a new product line.
Disturbance handlerInvoluntary response to pressures beyond the manager's control.A strike looms, a major customer goes bankrupt, raw material delayed by a road accident.
Resource allocatorDeciding who gets what: money, people, equipment, and most importantly the manager's own time; designing structure; authorising decisions.Budget distribution among departments.
NegotiatorSpends considerable time negotiating on behalf of the unit; part of the job.Negotiating a contract with a supplier or a union settlement.
Common confusion

Entrepreneur vs Disturbance handler. Both are about change. Entrepreneur = change by choice, the manager starts it. Disturbance handler = change forced on the manager, who must react. Monitor vs Disseminator vs Spokesperson: collect → pass inside → speak outside.

Quick key for classifying an activity (N24 Q1A asks you to give category + role)

If the activity is…CategoryRole
Attending a retirement function or ribbon-cuttingInterpersonalFigurehead
Training and motivating subordinates, hiringInterpersonalLeader
Meeting a manager from another company or department to exchange informationInterpersonalLiaison
Reading reports, scanning the market, asking staff for updatesInformationalMonitor
Holding a team briefing, forwarding an email with new policyInformationalDisseminator
Giving a press statement, presenting results to shareholdersInformationalSpokesperson
Starting a new project or product on one's own initiativeDecisionalEntrepreneur
Handling a strike, a machine breakdown, a supplier defaultDecisionalDisturbance handler
Deciding the budget split or the work scheduleDecisionalResource allocator
Bargaining with a union or supplier over price or termsDecisionalNegotiator
How the exam asked it

N24 · Q1A (4): a table of managerial activities; “with reference to Mintzberg's managerial roles, mention the role category and specific role.”
M26 · Q1A (3): “A hospital faces a sudden shortage of critical supplies during an emergency. (i) Assess which of Mintzberg's roles are most critical. (ii) Find out how the manager should prioritise actions. Suggest a step-by-step response plan using at least 3 roles.”

Model answer for M26 Q1A (hospital shortage)

(i) Most critical roles: Disturbance handler (the shortage is a sudden, involuntary pressure), Resource allocator (scarce supplies must be rationed) and Negotiator (securing emergency stock). Supporting roles: Liaison, Monitor, Disseminator, Spokesperson, Leader.

(ii) Priority and step-by-step plan:

1
Monitortake stock: what is short, how many hours are left, who has stock
→
2
Disturbance handlerdeclare the emergency, set a crisis team and protocol
→
3
Resource allocatorration critical items to life-saving needs first (ICU, OT, emergency)
→
4
Negotiator / Liaisoncall suppliers, nearby hospitals, district authorities for emergency supply
→
5
Disseminator / Spokespersonbrief staff on the rationing rules; update patients' families and the authorities
→
6
Leaderkeep staff calm and motivated; review and restore normal supply

Justification for the order: handle the crisis first (disturbance), allocate scarce resources by clinical priority, then negotiate to expand supply, and communicate throughout.

1.7 The external environment (supplementary note)

The slide for this topic is only a title; the lesson plan lists “External environment”. The textbook (Koontz and Weihrich) treats it as the forces outside the firm that managers cannot control but must respond to. This links straight back to the open system idea.

Economic

Inflation, interest rates, consumer income, taxes, competitors, supply and demand.

Technological

New machines, automation, AI, digital platforms; they change products and methods.

Social

Attitudes, values, expectations, demographics, consumer habits and the rising expectation of social responsibility.

Political and legal

Government policy, labour laws, environmental rules, trade policy and regulation (RBI for banks, FSSAI for food).

Ethical

Society's standards of right and wrong, covered in 1.9.

Stakeholders

Customers, suppliers, shareholders, community, creditors, each of whom can act on the firm.

Use these headings as the answer skeleton if asked “explain the external environment of a business”.

1.8 Social responsibility of managers (CSR) and its drivers

Asked in endsemD24 · Q1BN25 · Q1B
Start here: a simple picture

A neighbourhood shopkeeper follows the law and pays taxes: that is the legal and economic minimum. But if he also sponsors a school's sports day, keeps the street in front of his shop clean, and refuses to sell expired goods even when nobody would notice, he is going beyond what the law forces him to do. When a firm voluntarily does the right thing for society, that is social responsibility.

Definition

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) is a business firm's intention, beyond its legal and economic obligations, to do the right things and act in ways that are good for society. (Corporate = organised business; Social = everything dealing with people; Responsibility = accountability between the two.) CSR is also called “corporate citizenship” and may involve short-term costs with no immediate financial benefit in order to promote positive social and environmental change.

This definition assumes the business obeys the law and pursues economic interests, and it treats the business as a moral agent that must differentiate right from wrong.

Two views on responsibility

Classical (purely economic) view

Management's only social responsibility is to maximise profits (within the law).

Socioeconomic view

Responsibility goes beyond profits to include protecting and improving society's welfare.

Drivers of CSR (what pushes a company to behave responsibly)

The slide shows the drivers around the idea of brand equity (the value of a brand, determined by the consumer's perception of its quality and desirability) and lists these supporting points:

DriverHow it drives CSRExample
Brand equity and reputationResponsible behaviour raises consumers' perception of the brand; irresponsible behaviour destroys it.A firm known for ethical sourcing earns a premium and loyalty.
Employee satisfactionIncreased satisfaction leads to employee competence, which gives superior service delivery and customer satisfaction. People like to work for a decent employer.Fair pay, safe working conditions, welfare programmes, lower attrition.
Goodwill and trustIt takes decades to build goodwill and trust in the minds of customers and shareholders; CSR protects that asset.Long-term brand trust built through community programmes.
Ethical cultureAn ethically responsible culture reduces the chance of employees indulging in unfair practices by emphasising professionalism and transparency.Code of ethics, whistle-blower policy.
Socially responsible investment, communication and fairnessSocially responsible investments, effective communication, employee participation, fairness, promotions, adequate compensation and personal development.ESG-based investors preferring responsible companies.

Textbook add-ons you may also mention if asked to “explain in detail”: legal and regulatory pressure, investor expectations (ESG), customer and civil-society expectations, and long-term competitive advantage.

Example

Examples to quote. Hindustan Unilever's Project Shakti (rural women as direct sellers of hygiene products, 2001, from the Blue Ocean slides) shows business and social benefit together. Tata group's community and education programmes, and Infosys Foundation's work, are widely cited Indian examples of corporate citizenship.

How the exam asked it

D24 · Q1B (3): “A business firm's intentions, beyond its legal and economic obligations. What does this intention mean and what are the drivers that ensure these intentions being fulfilled?”
N25 · Q1B (3): “What is Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)? Explain the role of drivers of CSR in detail.”

How to write it in the exam

Definition (underline beyond legal and economic obligations) → one line on classical vs socioeconomic view → the five drivers in a table with one example each → closing line: CSR is an investment in long-term goodwill, not just a cost.

1.9 Ethics in managing: the three moral theories

Asked in endsemM25 · Q1BM26 · Q1BJ26 · Q1B
Start here: a simple picture

Your friend group has one ticket left for a concert. Three ways to decide who gets it: (1) Give it to whoever makes the group happiest overall (utilitarian: the best outcome for the most people). (2) Give it to the person who was promised it, because a promise is a right nobody can take away (rights). (3) Draw lots or give it to the person who has never got a turn: whatever is fair and impartial (justice). Business ethics uses the same three lenses to judge plans and actions.

Definition

Ethics is “the discipline dealing with what is good and bad and with moral duty and obligation”. Business ethics is a systematic study of morals; it gives methods to distinguish actions and attitudes that harm business from those that are ethically sound.

The three basic types of moral theory (normative ethics)

1. Utilitarian theory

Plans and actions should be evaluated by their consequences. They should produce the greatest good for the greatest number of people.

Test: who benefits and who is harmed overall?

2. Theory based on rights

All people have basic rights, such as freedom of conscience, free speech and due process; these must be respected whatever the consequences.

Test: whose right is being violated?

3. Theory of justice

Decision-makers must be guided by fairness, equity and impartiality.

Test: is everyone treated fairly and equally?

The slide's example sets (learn to classify them)

ExampleTheoryWhy
A tech company ensures user data privacy by refusing to sell personal informationRightsRight to privacy.
A media company protects journalists' right to publish unbiased reports without censorshipRightsFree speech.
A firm provides employees paid leave for votingRightsCivic rights of employees.
A corporation ensures equal pay for the same work regardless of gender or backgroundJusticeEquity and impartiality.
A retailer adopts a fair-pricing policy so small vendors are treated equitablyJusticeFairness to vendors.
A school gives scholarships to economically disadvantaged studentsJusticePromotes fairness.
A company runs a recycling programme that benefits the whole communityUtilitarianGreatest good for the many.
A pharma firm prices a life-saving drug affordably to maximise accessibilityUtilitarianBenefit for most people.
A manufacturer shuts down a high-polluting unit to protect the health of surrounding communitiesUtilitarianLong-term good of the many.

Institutionalising ethics: turning theory into daily practice

Top managers must create an environment that fosters ethical decision-making, by applying and integrating ethical concepts into daily actions. The slide gives three ways:

1
Code of ethicsan appropriate company policy or code of ethics
→
2
Ethics committeea formally appointed committee to review issues and handle violations
→
3
Ethics trainingteaching ethics in management development programmes

Linking frameworks to company practice (for the “real-world examples” part). Utilitarian: a code that weighs a plant's profit against community health (closing a polluting unit). Rights: data-privacy and freedom-of-speech policies, whistle-blower protection. Justice: pay-equity audits, transparent promotion criteria, anti-discrimination policy. Then show the three institutional tools: a published code of ethics, an ethics committee, ethics modules in leadership training.

Common confusion

Many students confuse Rights with Justice. Rights = protecting what each individual is entitled to. Justice = distributing benefits and burdens fairly among people. If the case talks about “equal”, “fair”, “equitable” → justice. If it talks about “right to”, “freedom”, “privacy”, “due process” → rights.

How the exam asked it

M25 · Q1B (3) and M26 · Q1B (3): “Critically analyse the three fundamental moral theories in normative ethics and their role in fostering ethical decision-making within organisations. Using real-world examples, demonstrate how companies can institutionalise ethics through these frameworks.”
J26 · Q1B (3): “Analyse the three basic moral theories in normative ethics.”

1.10 Trust as the basis for change management

Start here: a simple picture

When a new school principal changes the timetable, students who trust her assume there must be a good reason and adapt quickly. Where there is no trust, every change triggers suspicion and resistance. Trust is the oil that lets an organisation change without grinding.

Definition

Change management is a systematic approach to dealing with the transition or transformation of an organisation's goals, processes and technologies. Its purpose is to implement strategies for effecting and controlling change and helping people adapt to it.

  • Managers are bombarded with new management concepts (and old ones disguised with new names) to cope with global competition, customer expectations and the need to respond quickly.
  • The often-overlooked concept is trust: it is at the centre of communication, collaboration and the willingness to change.
  • Traditionally trust is equated with integrity, loyalty, caring and keeping promises between individuals.
  • It should extend to the organisation through a culture of trust that transcends individual leadership: leaders come and go; the organisation continues.

1.11 International business and management across cultures

Asked in endsemN24 · Q1BJ25 · Q1BD25 · Q1B
Start here: a simple picture

The same joke can get a laugh in one country and a frown in another. In the same way, a management style that works perfectly in one culture (say, quick individual decisions in the USA) can fail in another (where group agreement is expected, as in Japan). Managers who work abroad must read the cultural environment first.

Five dimensions of national culture (Hofstede-type)

A country's culture shapes employee behaviour and therefore management practice. The slides group behaviours into five dimensions, each shown with a visual:

DimensionMeaningEffect on managementIllustration
1. Individualism vs collectivismIndividual interests and achievement vs group harmony and loyaltyIndividual targets and rewards vs team goals and consensusUSA individualist; Japan, Korea collectivist
2. Large vs small power distanceHow far less powerful members accept unequal powerHierarchical, top-down instructions vs participative, flat structuresKorea large; Scandinavian countries small
3. Uncertainty tolerance vs avoidanceComfort with ambiguity and risk vs need for rules and certaintyRapid innovation and risk-taking vs detailed procedures and cautious changeItaly, Austria low risk tolerance; Australia and USA more risk-taking
4. Masculinity vs femininityAggressive vs passive goal behaviour (assertiveness and achievement vs caring and quality of life)Competitive, results-driven vs cooperative, relationship-drivenUsed in the slides as aggressive vs passive goal behaviour
5. Short-term vs long-term orientationFocus on quick results vs persistence and future rewardsQuarterly profit focus vs long-term investment and lifetime employmentUSA short-term; Japan long-term

Illustrations are indicative; always state them as “typically” in an exam.

Country sketches given in the slides

  • German: favoured reliance on authority, often benevolent authoritarianism; managers show concern for subordinates but expect obedience.
  • Austrian: self-realisation and leadership; independence and competitiveness valued; tolerance for risk-taking low.
  • Australian: moralistic stance, emphasis on political and social values, achievement and risk-taking.
  • Italian: low tolerance for risk; very competitive but like group decision-making.
  • British: job security, resourcefulness, adaptability, logic; individualism highly valued.

Korean vs Japanese vs American management (the table the exam copies from)

AspectKoreanJapaneseAmerican
Decision-makingTop-down, hierarchicalConsensus-driven, participativeTop-down, fast, individual
Employment practicesLoyalty and seniorityLifetime employment, loyaltyPerformance-based, employee mobility
CommunicationIndirect, high-contextIndirect, high-contextDirect, low-context
Workplace relationshipsHierarchy, respect for eldersGroup harmony and team cohesionIndividualism, personal achievement
Leadership styleAuthoritative, paternalisticFacilitative, consensus-orientedAuthoritative, results-oriented
MotivationLoyalty to company, respect for authorityGroup harmony, job securityIndividual achievement, rewards
Conflict resolutionAvoidance, maintaining faceAvoidance, maintaining harmonyConfrontational, quick resolution
Training and developmentExtensive in-house, seniority-basedIn-house, long-term orientationFormal education, continuous professional development
Innovation and changeSlow to adopt, cautiousIncremental improvements, cautiousRapid adoption, proactive
Work-life balanceLong hours, high dedicationLong hours, strong commitmentEmphasis on balance, flexible hours
Performance evaluationSeniority and loyaltyGroup performance and seniorityIndividual performance, results-oriented
CSREmerging importanceHigh importance, integrated into businessHigh importance, driven by stakeholders and regulations

Theory Z (William Ouchi, 1980s): the blend

Theory Z integrates Japanese and American practices. The Japanese emphasis is on collective decision-making; the American emphasis is on individual responsibility. Theory Z focuses on increasing employee loyalty by providing a job for life with strong concern for employee well-being on and off the job, and tends to promote stable employment, high productivity and high employee morale.

FeatureJapanese (J)American (A)Theory Z
EmploymentLifetimeShort-termLong-term
Decision-makingCollectiveIndividualConsensual, participative
ResponsibilityCollectiveIndividualIndividual
Evaluation and promotionSlowRapidSlow
ControlImplicitExplicitImplicit and informal, with explicit formal measures
Career pathNon-specialisedSpecialisedModerately specialised
Concern for employeeHolisticSegmented (as an employee only)Holistic, including family
How the exam asked it

N24 · Q1B and J25 · Q1B (3): “Compare and contrast the managerial practices in Japan and the USA, focusing on cultural influences and organisational behaviour.”
D25 · Q1B (3): “Analyse three cultural dimensions that can influence management practices and employee behaviour in a multinational company operating across diverse countries. Give one example for each.”

How to write it in the exam

For Japan vs USA: write a 6 to 7 row comparison table (decision-making, employment, communication, relationships, leadership, motivation, evaluation), then one paragraph linking each to culture (collectivism vs individualism, long-term vs short-term). Add a closing line on Theory Z. For the cultural dimensions question: name any three of the five, define each, and give one MNC example (say, a power-distance example from a firm operating in India and Sweden).

End of chapter

Chapter 1: summary

  • Business vs industry: a business is one company aiming at profit by providing goods (tangible) and services (intangible); an industry is a group of such firms. Four types: primary (extract), secondary (manufacture), tertiary (service), quaternary (research and knowledge).
  • Managers direct others' work. Three levels: top (administrative: strategy), middle (executory: tactics), lower (supervisory: day-to-day). Three skills: technical, human, conceptual. Human is needed at every level; conceptual rises with rank; technical falls.
  • Five functions: planning, organising, staffing, leading, controlling, with communication throughout.
  • Systems approach: the organisation is an open system of interdependent sub-systems: inputs → transformation (the five functions) → outputs, with feedback, inside an external environment.
  • Fayol's 14 principles: division of labour, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, equity, order, discipline, initiative, fair remuneration, stability of tenure, scalar chain (gang plank), subordination of individual interest, esprit de corps, centralisation/decentralisation.
  • Mintzberg's 10 roles: Interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison); Informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson); Decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).
  • CSR: a firm's intention, beyond its legal and economic obligations, to do good for society. Drivers: brand equity, employee satisfaction, goodwill and trust, ethical culture, responsible investment.
  • Ethics: three moral theories: utilitarian (greatest good for the greatest number), rights (basic rights), justice (fairness and equity). Institutionalise through a code, an ethics committee and ethics training.
  • Trust is the foundation of change management: communication, collaboration and willingness to change depend on it.
  • International business: five cultural dimensions; Japan is consensus-driven and long-term; the USA is individual and short-term; Korea is hierarchical; Theory Z blends Japanese and American practice.

Most likely exam items from this chapter: Fayol with case lines · Mintzberg classification or a scenario · systems approach diagram · three moral theories with examples · CSR drivers · Japan vs USA table.

Chapter 2

Essentials of Planning

Lectures 9–17 · Types of plans · Steps in planning · Objectives · MBO · Strategies and policies · Quality · Critical question analysis · Blue Ocean · SWOT and TOWS · BCG matrix · Porter's generic strategies

2.1 What is planning and why it matters

Start here: a simple picture

You would never start a road trip from Manipal to Goa without deciding the route, the stops, the budget for petrol and the time you must reach by. That list is a plan. Without it you may still reach somewhere, but not necessarily Goa, and not on time. Planning is deciding in advance where you are, where you want to be, and how to bridge the gap.

Definition

A plan is a blueprint for goal achievement: it specifies the necessary resource allocations, schedules, tasks and other actions needed to achieve the purpose. Planning involves selecting missions and objectives and the actions to achieve them, which requires decision-making, that is choosing among alternatives.

Planning answers six basic questions about any activity

1
What needs to be accomplished?and what are the alternative routes
→
2
When is the deadline?
→
3
Where will it be done?
→
4
Who will be responsible?
→
5
How will it get done?
→
6
How much time, energy and resources are required?

Why planning is important

  • Helps management clarify, focus and research the business or project's development and prospects.
  • Provides a considered and logical framework within which a business can develop and pursue its goals.
  • Offers a benchmark against which actual performance can be measured and reviewed (this is why control needs planning).
  • Helps avoid mistakes and recognise hidden opportunities.
  • Guides development of products, management, finances, markets and competition.
  • Helps in forecasting the future and makes it visible to some extent.
  • Bridges where we are and where we want to be.

2.2 Types of plans (the eight kinds)

Asked in endsemN24 · Q1CD24 · Q1CJ25 · Q1CN25 · Q2AD25 · Q1CM26 · Q1C
Start here: a simple picture

You are running your college annual fest. Mission: “to celebrate student talent”. Objective: “sell 2,000 tickets and earn a ₹3 lakh surplus”. Strategy: “partner with sponsors and use Instagram influencers”. Policy: “always choose local vendors where possible”. Procedure: “vendor registration → approval → payment”. Rule: “no entry without ID card”. Programme: the full fest schedule, volunteer allocation and publicity. Budget: “₹1.5 lakh for stage, ₹50,000 for publicity…”. That is the whole ladder, from the big idea to the rupee numbers.

All managers at all levels plan, but the plans made by a top-level manager differ from those made by lower-level managers, and plans differ in what they seek to achieve and the methods used. The slides list eight types of plans:

1. Purpose / mission / vision

Identifies the basic function or task of an enterprise (or any part of it). Examples from the slides: an oil company: “to search for oil and to produce, refine and market petroleum products”; DuPont: “better things through chemistry”. (Mission = what we do and for whom; vision = what we want to become.)

2. Goals / objectives

The important ends towards which organisational and individual activities are directed. Verifiable objectives allow measurement of the surplus as well as the effectiveness and efficiency of managerial action. Example: “earn a 10% profit on the amount invested in the first year”.

3. Strategy

A complete and all-inclusive plan for achieving objectives. It has three dimensions: (1) establishing long-term objectives, (2) selecting a specific course of action, (3) allocating the necessary resources. Strategy formation is generally reserved for top management. Example: “enter tier-2 cities through a low-cost delivery model”.

4. Policy

A general statement or understanding that guides or channels thinking in decision-making. Not all policies are written; many are merely implied from managers' actions (e.g. the practice of promoting from within). Policies define an area within which a decision is to be made, ensure the decision is consistent with the objective, and decide issues before they become problems. Examples: hire university-trained engineers; promote from within; set competitive prices; buy from the lowest of three qualified bidders; encourage employee suggestions.

5. Procedure

A stepwise guide for routine activities, in chronological order, followed by all employees. Examples: admission of a student: application form → collection of documents → sorting of applications; the procedure to implement a vacation policy (scheduling leave to avoid disruption).

6. Rules

Very specific statements that define an action or non-action. They allow no flexibility, they are final, must be followed by all, and violation has consequences. They are the simplest type of plan, guide actions without specifying time sequence, and may or may not be part of a procedure. Examples: no-smoking zone, no-phone zone, ₹100 fine per day for not wearing a cap.

7. Programmes

A complex of goals, policies, procedures, rules, task assignments, steps to be taken, resources to be employed and other elements needed to carry out a given course of action; ordinarily supported by budgets. Examples: a 5-year plan to build a plant; a rural digital-literacy training programme.

8. Budgets

A statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms; “numberised programmes”. May be in labour hours, units of production, rupees, machine-hours. Types on the slide: variable (flexible) budgets (depend on the level of output), programme budgets (each department identifies its goals), and zero-based budgets (each package costed from zero; see 5.12).

The three confusing ones: policy vs procedure vs rule

PolicyProcedureRule
What it doesGuides thinkingGives steps in sequenceAllows or forbids an action
FlexibilitySome discretion within limitsFollow the stepsNone
Time sequenceNoYes (chronological)No
Example“Promote from within”“Application → documents → interview → offer”“No mobile phones on the shop floor”
Remember this

Keyword cheat for case questions: “goal / target / aims to achieve X%” → Objective. “Credit terms, only from…, always prefer…” → Policy. “Steps / step-by-step / first … then … finally” → Procedure. “Penalty / not allowed / must not / strict” → Rule. “Marketing strategy targeting…” / “plan to expand into…” → Strategy. “Complex plan with training, resources, schedule” → Programme. “Annual budget of ₹…” / “statement of workers required” → Budget.

Other ways of classifying plans (perspectives)

The slides say the most popular ways to describe plans are by content, breadth, time frame, specificity and frequency of use. These classifications are not mutually exclusive (one plan can be strategic, long-term, directional and single-use at once).

PerspectiveTwo kindsDifference
Content / breadthStrategic vs tactical (and operational)Strategic: whole organisation, set overall objectives, position the organisation in its environment, cover extended periods (five or more years), less specific. Tactical: specific parts of the organisation, derived from strategic objectives, detail how objectives will be achieved, cover shorter periods, updated continuously. Operational: limited in scope, measured daily, weekly or monthly.
Time frameLong-term vs short-termLong-term: beyond five years, what the organisation wants to become, great uncertainty, set by higher levels. Short-term: up to one year, basis for day-to-day operations; answers “are we doing things right?”.
SpecificityDirectional vs specificDirectional: flexible, general guidelines (“go from here to there”). Specific: clearly defined objectives, no room for misinterpretation (what, when, where, how much, by whom).
Frequency of useSingle-use vs standingSingle-use: for a unique situation (one-day sales advertisement, a project). Standing: ongoing guidance for repeated actions (a customer satisfaction policy).

Model answer: D24 Q1C (top vs lower plans — six types)

Take one company (say an automobile maker) and show how each type appears at each level: Mission (top): “provide affordable, safe mobility”. Objective (top/middle): “15% market share in 3 years”. Strategy (top): “low-cost compact cars through lean manufacturing”. Policy (middle): “source parts from local suppliers where quality equals”. Procedure (lower): “inspection steps on the assembly line”. Rule (lower): “helmets and safety shoes compulsory on the shop floor”. Add a line: top-level plans are broad, long-term and unstructured; lower-level plans are narrow, short-term and highly specific.

2.3 The steps in planning (the eight-step process)

Asked in endsemM25 · Q1C
Start here: a simple picture

Planning a wedding follows the same order every time: you notice an opportunity (a date is available), decide the goal (200 guests, ₹10 lakh budget), assume conditions (season, guest list), list alternatives (hall vs lawn vs resort), compare them, pick one, plan supporting arrangements (caterer, decorator, transport) and finally put numbers on everything (the budget). Business planning runs the same eight steps.

1
Being aware of opportunitiesmarket, competition, customers' needs, our strengths and weaknesses
→
2
Setting objectives / goalswhere we want to be and what we want to accomplish
→
3
Considering planning premisesin what environment (internal and external) will plans operate
→
4
Identifying alternativesthe most promising ways to accomplish the objectives
→
5
Comparing alternativesin the light of the goals sought
→
6
Choosing an alternativeselecting the course of action we will pursue
→
7
Formulating supporting plansbuy equipment, buy materials, hire and train workforce, develop a product
→
8
Numberising plans by budgetsvolume and price of sales, operating expenses, capital expenditure
StepQuestion it answersInventory-management example (M25 Q1C)
1. Awareness of opportunitiesIn light of market, competition, customers' needs, strengths and weaknesses?Frequent stock-outs of fast-moving items; supplier lead times vary; competitors deliver faster.
2. Setting objectivesWhere do we want to be?Cut stock-outs to under 2%; reduce holding cost by 10% in the next financial year.
3. Planning premisesIn what environment will plans operate?Forecast demand, lead time of 7 days, price inflation of raw materials, available warehouse space.
4. Identifying alternativesWhat are the most promising routes?EOQ, just-in-time, safety stock, vendor-managed inventory.
5. Comparing alternativesWhich best meets goals at lowest cost and highest profit?Compare cost, risk of stock-out and supplier dependence of each.
6. ChoosingWhich course will we follow?ABC analysis with EOQ for A items and JIT for fast movers.
7. Supporting plansWhat else must be planned?Purchase plan, warehouse layout, training for stores staff, software for stock tracking.
8. Numberising (budgets)What will it cost, in numbers?Purchase budget, working-capital budget, storage-cost budget.
How the exam asked it

M25 · Q1C (3): “As the Supply Manager … develop an 8-step planning process for inventory management that enhances efficiency, cost-effectiveness and resource utilisation.”

How to write it in the exam

Write the eight steps by name (use exactly the slide names above) and give one inventory line against each. A 8-box flow chart plus a two-column table scores fully.

2.4 Objectives: the hierarchy, multiplicity and what makes them verifiable

Start here: a simple picture

Your semester goal: “score well”. That is a wish. “Score 8.5 CGPA by end of this semester, with at least 80% in management” is an objective: you can check whether you achieved it. The more specific an objective, the easier it is to plan for and to measure.

  • Hierarchy of objectives: from socio-economic purpose, mission and overall objectives at the top, to division, department and individual objectives at the bottom. They are linked in a network, each supporting the one above.
  • Top-down approach: upper-level managers determine the objectives for subordinates. Bottom-up approach: subordinates initiate objectives. (MBO combines the two.)
  • Multiplicity of objectives: a business has several objectives at each level because it must satisfy owners, employees, consumers, creditors, vendors, society and others, so separate objectives are set for each group.
Quantitative objectives

Easy to measure, numerical, concrete, observable.
Increase annual revenue by 10%; reduce production costs by 15%.

Qualitative objectives

Hard to measure; not numerical.
Enhance customer experience and satisfaction; improve brand reputation.

Verifiable vs non-verifiable objectives (slide examples)

Non-verifiable (vague)Verifiable (measurable, time-bound)
To make a reasonable profitTo achieve a return on investment of 12% at the end of the current fiscal year
To improve communicationTo issue a two-page monthly newsletter from July 1, with not more than 40 work hours of preparation time
To improve productivityTo increase production output by 5% by December 31 without additional cost and maintaining quality
To develop better managersTo conduct a 40-hour in-house “Fundamentals of Management” programme this year, with 90% of managers passing
To install a computer systemTo install a computerised control system in production by December 31, within 500 working hours, with not more than 10% downtime in the first 3 months
Remember this

A verifiable objective answers: how much, by when, at what cost/quality. The same idea reappears as SMART goals in 2.7.

2.5 Management by Objectives (MBO)

Asked in endsemJ26 · Q1C
Start here: a simple picture

Imagine a coach who sits down with each player before the season, and together they agree: “you will score 15 goals, I will give you training and a regular place”. They review progress mid-season and at the end. The player knows exactly what is expected, feels ownership because he helped decide it, and is measured fairly. That is MBO: objectives agreed by both manager and subordinate, then measured against results.

Definition

Management by Objectives (MBO) is a comprehensive managerial system that integrates many key managerial activities in a systematic manner and is consciously directed toward the effective and efficient achievement of organisational and individual objectives. It was popularised by Peter Drucker in his 1954 book The Practice of Management; it is also called “management by planning”. Managers and employees define performance objectives for every department, project and person, and use them to monitor performance.

Features of organisational objectives in MBO

  • Verifiable and quantified.
  • Hierarchy of objectives.
  • Network of objectives.
  • Multiplicity of objectives.
  • A process of objective-setting that runs through the organisational hierarchy.

MBO emphasises performance appraisal, short-term objectives and motivation, and long-term planning.

The process of MBO

1
Enterprise objectives and key result areasset top-level goals, planning premises
→
2
Superior's preliminary recommendationobjectives for the subordinate
→
3
Subordinate's preliminary statementhis own objectives and the resources needed
→
4
Agreementsuperior and subordinate settle the final objectives
→
5
Ongoing performancesubordinate works; superior reviews periodically
→
6
Corrective measures and assistancefrom superior
→
7
Final review and appraisalof performance, new inputs for the next cycle

Key result areas (Drucker)

A key result area is an area in which performance is essential for the success of the enterprise. Drucker's eight: market standing, innovation, productivity, physical and financial resources, profitability, managerial performance and development, worker performance and attitude, public responsibility. Additional areas on the slide: service and quality.

Setting employee objectives

  1. Identify the employee's key job tasks.
  2. Establish specific and challenging goals for each key task.
  3. Allow the employee to participate actively.
  4. Prioritise goals.
  5. Build in feedback mechanisms.
  6. Link rewards to goal attainment.

Objectives of MBO

To identify problems and opportunities; convert opportunities into clear goals; set up a system to turn goals into achievements; review the organisation in the light of objectives; establish objectives of each job and unit; clarify the policies and systems to accomplish them; set up a review system.

Benefits (advantages)
  • The need for planning is recognised.
  • Provides objectives and accountability for performance.
  • Encourages participative management.
  • Helps in job enrichment.
  • Provides a good feedback system.
  • Leader and subordinate efforts focus on activities leading to goal attainment.
  • Performance improves up and down the chain; motivated people.
Weaknesses (limitations)
  • Failure to teach the philosophy of MBO.
  • Failure to give guidelines to goal setters.
  • Difficulty of setting goals.
  • Emphasis on short-run goals.
  • Danger of inflexibility.
  • Over-quantifying: using numbers where they do not apply.

Problems: change adversely affects planning; low morale reduces effectiveness; lower-level goals take precedence; over-centralised authority limits participation; paperwork.

Relevance in modern organisations (the “relevance” part of J26's question): the logic of MBO is alive in performance-management systems, KPIs/KRAs and OKRs (objectives and key results), and in goal-setting in agile and start-up teams. Its weaknesses (rigidity, paperwork, over-focus on numbers) are handled today by quarterly resets, frequent feedback and balanced scorecards. (Add-on beyond the slides, useful as a closing paragraph.)

How the exam asked it

J26 · Q1C (3): “Analyse Management by Objectives (MBO) as proposed by Peter Drucker. Discuss its advantages, limitations and relevance in modern organisations.”

2.6 Strategies, policies and the strategic planning process

Asked in endsemN24 · Q2AJ25 · Q2A
Start here: a simple picture

Think of a cricket team before a tournament. The captain does not decide each ball in advance; he decides the big approach: “we win through pace bowling at home, spin abroad; we rotate the squad to keep key players fit”. That broad, long-term approach is the strategy. Standing instructions such as “always bat first on a dry pitch” are policies.

Multiplicity and the three levels of strategy

A strategy is a plan with three dimensions: long-term objectives, a specific course of action, and allocation of resources. The slide splits strategy into three levels:

LevelQuestion it answersWho decidesExample
Corporate-levelWhat business(es) are we in?Top managementTata group deciding to be in steel, cars, IT and hotels.
Business-level (competitive)How do we compete?Business unit headsA car unit competing on low cost, or on premium features.
Functional-levelHow do we support the business-level strategy?Functional managersHR hires for skills the strategy needs; marketing designs the promotion.

The strategic planning process

Strategic planning is the process of developing the strategy or direction and an action plan to achieve the goals of an organisation. The slide's framework flows like this:

1
Inputspeople, capital, managerial skills, technology
→
2
Top management's orientationvalues and vision; present and future
→
3
Environmental scanexternal threats and opportunities (industry analysis) and internal strengths and weaknesses
→
4
Purpose and major objectives of the enterprise
→
5
Development of alternate strategies
→
6
Strategic choice
→
7
Medium- and short-run planningand re-engineering structure, staffing, leadership
→
8
Implementation, evaluation and controlwith consistency testing and contingency planning

The slide groups the tools to develop strategy into five related-but-distinct methods; a manager can use any one, or a combination:

1. Critical question analysis

Asking a set of probing questions about the business and customers.

2. SWOT and TOWS

Analyse internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats, and turn them into strategies.

3. Blue Ocean strategy

Create new, uncontested market space.

4. Business portfolio (BCG)

Allocate resources across business units by growth and share.

5. Porter's generic model

Choose cost leadership, differentiation or focus.

How the exam asked it

N24 · Q2A and J25 · Q2A (4): “As the leader of the organisation … Proficiency in several tools and methodologies is necessary [for a strategic plan]. Using appropriate representation and examples, discuss any two strategic tools that you will implement to facilitate the development of your firm.”

How to write it in the exam

Pick any two that you can draw. The safest pair is SWOT/TOWS (draw the 2×2 and the 3×3 strategy matrix) and BCG matrix (draw the 2×2 with stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs). For each: one-line definition, diagram, a 4-line example from a real company, and one line on how it helps strategy development. Both are covered below with ready diagrams.

2.7 Quality management, TQM and SMART quality goals (course-plan topic)

Lectures 11 and 12 in the course plan cover quality management, but the slide deck contains no slides for them (they are partly self-directed learning, SDL). This section gives you the standard textbook content so nothing in the lesson plan is left uncovered. It has not appeared in the 8 papers so far.

Start here: a simple picture

A restaurant that fixes a wrongly-cooked dish only when a customer complains is practising inspection. A restaurant that studies why dishes go wrong, trains the cooks, improves the recipe cards and asks diners for feedback every week is practising total quality management: quality is built into the process and everyone owns it.

Definition

Total Quality Management (TQM) is a management approach in which every employee and every process is committed to continuously improving quality, with the aim of long-term success through customer satisfaction.

  • Customer focus: quality is defined by the customer.
  • Continuous improvement (Kaizen): small, ongoing improvements in all processes.
  • Employee involvement: everyone is responsible for quality.
  • Process approach and data-based decisions: use measurement and statistical tools (the seven QC tools).
  • Leadership commitment and supplier partnership.

Strategic quality planning and SMART quality goals

Strategic quality planning builds quality targets into the organisation's strategic plan. Good quality goals are SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Example: “reduce customer-reported defects from 4% to 2% within 12 months”. Aligning with MBO means each department's quality goal is agreed with the manager, linked to rewards, and reviewed periodically, exactly the MBO cycle in 2.5.

Standards that support quality: ISO 9000 (quality management systems), ISO 14000 (environmental management).

2.8 Critical question analysis

Start here: a simple picture

Before a shop-owner decides to expand, she asks herself: What exactly do I sell? Who buys it? Why do they buy from me? What will they want next year? These honest questions often show that the business is not what she thought. That is critical question analysis.

It asks a set of key questions to define the business and its strategy:

  • What is our business? Who are our customers? What do our customers want?
  • How much will our customers buy and at what price?
  • Do we wish to be a product leader? Do we wish to develop our own new products?
Example

Slide example: glass-bottle manufacturers missed opportunities by seeing themselves for too long as glass bottle makers rather than liquid container manufacturers, while plastic and metal containers replaced glass in many cases. Answering “What is our business?” correctly would have saved them.

Marketing-strategy questions (slide): Where are our customers and why do they buy? How do our customers buy? How is it best for us to sell? Do we have something to offer that competitors do not?

2.9 Blue Ocean strategy

Asked in endsemM26 · Q2A
Start here: a simple picture

Picture a lake full of fishing boats competing for the same fish (a red ocean: crowded, bloody competition). Now imagine rowing to a different, untouched part of the sea where nobody fishes yet and the fish are plentiful (a blue ocean). Instead of beating the others, you make them irrelevant. Cirque du Soleil did this: it did not fight circuses on price; it created a new kind of entertainment.

Definition

Blue Ocean Strategy (W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne) is a business approach that encourages companies to create new market spaces instead of competing in saturated markets. Success lies in “blue oceans”: untapped, uncontested market space ripe for growth. It stresses the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost to open a new market space and create new demand, making competition irrelevant.

Two pivot principles

1. Value innovation

Delivering superior value to customers through differentiation and low cost together; beating competition by making it irrelevant, redefining industry boundaries.

2. Creation of uncontested market space

Instead of fighting for a share of existing demand, create new demand in a space with no rivals.

The Four Actions Framework (ERRC grid)

To create value innovation, the slides classify the factors / attributes / features / services in the industry into four groups:

In the strategy canvas / competitive-factor analysis, you compare competitors on their evaluation factors and see where a new value curve can break away from the crowd.

Advantages
  • Create new demand and tap new markets.
  • Focus on unique value propositions that appeal to customers.
  • Avoid cut-throat competition of traditional markets.
  • Achieve sustained profitability.
Challenges
  • High risk of failure.
  • Significant resource investment.
  • Uncertainty of unexplored markets.

Applications given in the slides

  • Hindustan Unilever, Project Shakti (2001): rural India got basic hygiene and sanitation products through a direct-selling model, increasing sales while serving unmet needs.
  • Airtel: mobile banking services (2010).
  • Flipkart: began as a small start-up competing with big players, focused on the needs of the Indian consumer; later expanded into grocery delivery (2015).

Blue Ocean vs Porter's generic model (the M26 comparison)

Porter's generic strategiesBlue Ocean strategy
Core logicCompete inside an existing industry, with a trade-off between low cost or differentiationBreak the trade-off: low cost and differentiation together
MarketExisting market space (red ocean)New, uncontested space (blue ocean)
CompetitionBeat the competitionMake competition irrelevant
Both cost and differentiation?Risks being “stuck in the middle” with no advantagePossible and intended, through value innovation
Industry boundariesTaken as givenRedefined
How the exam asked it

M26 · Q2A (3): “Porter's generic model suggests that a company attempting to engage in both cost leadership and differentiation simultaneously risks being ‘stuck in the middle’ … Contrast this with the Blue Ocean Strategy, which explicitly pivots on ‘value innovation’.”

How to write it in the exam

Open with Porter's trade-off and stuck in the middle, then Blue Ocean's two principles, then the table above, then an example (Project Shakti: low-cost small sachets plus differentiation of reaching rural women, creating a new market). Close with a note that Blue Ocean carries risk and investment.

2.10 SWOT analysis and the TOWS matrix

Asked in endsemD25 · Q2AJ26 · Q2A
Start here: a simple picture

A student preparing for exams does a quick self-check: strengths (good at maths), weaknesses (poor at theory subjects), opportunities (a free online course, a helpful senior), threats (too many assignments, a clash of exam dates). SWOT lists them. TOWS then asks: how do I use my strengths to grab opportunities, fix weaknesses by using opportunities, use strengths against threats, and minimise both weaknesses and threats? SWOT is the diagnosis; TOWS is the treatment plan.

SWOT analysis

An acronym for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats; credited to Albert Humphrey, who led a research project at Stanford University in the 1960s and 70s. A planning tool used to understand the SWOT of a project or business, and a framework for organising data from situation analysis of the internal and external environment.

Strengths

Characteristics that give an advantage over others; positive tangible and intangible attributes, internal: human competencies, process capabilities, financial resources, products and services, customer goodwill and brand loyalty. Examples: abundant finance, well-known brand, economies of scale, lower costs, superior management talent, committed employees.

Weaknesses

Characteristics that place the firm at a disadvantage; detract from its ability to attain the core goal. They are controllable: must be minimised and eliminated. Examples: limited finance, weak R&D spend, narrow product line, limited distribution, higher costs, out-of-date technology, weak market image, under-trained employees.

Opportunities

Chances to make greater profit; external attractive factors that give a reason to exist and develop; can arise from market, competition, industry/government and technology. Examples: rapid market growth, complacent rivals, changing customer tastes, new uses of the product, economic boom, deregulation.

Threats

External elements that could cause trouble; beyond the organisation's control; conditions that jeopardise reliability and profitability. Worse when they combine with weaknesses. Examples: foreign competitors, substitutes, declining product life cycle, rival strategies, more regulation, economic downturn.

Example

Slide exercise: an EV launch by a car maker. S: eco-friendly, silent engine, simpler mechanism, low maintenance, cheaper to run, energy saved by regenerative braking. W: high price, long recharge time, expensive battery change, lack of charging infrastructure. O: huge untapped EV market, rising green-technology demand, rising fuel costs, lower taxes, government subsidies. T: entry of competitors, rising electricity cost, hybrid vehicles adding to competition.

The TOWS matrix

Definition

TOWS analysis interlinks a company's internal strengths and weaknesses with the threats and opportunities in its external environment. It is a categorisation of the strategies available, by aligning internal elements with external factors. It gives four alternative strategies: SO, ST, WO and WT.

Common confusion

Retrenchment strategy (WT): reducing the diversity or overall size of operations, typically withdrawing from certain markets or discontinuing products or services to cut expenses and become financially more stable, with the goal of a beneficial turnaround.

The Apple story: one example for each TOWS cell (slide)

CellApple example
SOStrong brand loyalty + product design strength combined with the growing popularity of touchscreen smartphones led to the first iPhone, an immediate and massive hit.
STStrengths in design and brand loyalty let Apple keep a proprietary Lightning connector while others adopted Type-C. Facing the EU threat (regulators pushing Type-C), it relies on design strength and loyalty to keep customers buying official accessories.
WOA smaller product portfolio and not always being quickest to follow trends (weakness) + the wearables boom from about 2010 (opportunity) → Apple overcame its weakness and launched Apple Watch in 2015, a success.
WTApple TV (since 2007) never succeeded commercially because of limited functionality and interconnectivity (weakness), while streaming competition grew (threat). Launching Apple TV+ reduced the weakness and met the threat.

Dynamics of the TOWS matrix (J26)

The TOWS matrix is not static. The slide draws it as a series of matrices over time: Past → Present → Present + T1 → Present + T2. The firm's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats keep shifting, so the strategy mix must be re-run.
