A WO strategy can turn into a high-success SO strategy: once the company overcomes a weakness by capitalising on an opportunity, the weakness becomes a strength, and the opportunity becomes a platform for further SO moves.

Example

Example (Apple): Then (WO): weakness = narrow portfolio and late to wearables; opportunity = growing wearables market → Apple Watch (2015). Later (SO): the Watch, with its health features, becomes a strength; combined with Apple's brand loyalty and ecosystem, it supports further SO moves such as more health-monitoring features. Generic version: a start-up weak in distribution (W) uses the e-commerce boom (O) to build an online channel (WO); once that channel is strong (S), it uses it to enter new cities (SO).

How the exam asked it

D25 · Q2A (4): “Zomato … Perform a SWOT analysis for Zomato and create two TOWS strategies to capitalise on the opportunities.” (12 statements given.)
J26 · Q2A (4): “Explain the ‘Dynamics of the TOWS Matrix’ in relation to a company's progression through time. Specifically, analyse how a WO strategy can eventually transition into a high-success SO strategy. Use a suitable example to show how a company overcame its initial weakness.”

Worked answer: D25 Q2A (Zomato)
QuadrantStatements from the case
Strengths(i) strong brand recognition and loyal customer base; (v) wide range of services; (ix) advanced technology platform for real-time tracking and logistics
Weaknesses(ii) high operational costs, dependence on third-party delivery staff; (vi) limited profitability despite high revenue due to discounting; (x) vulnerability to service-quality issues affecting brand image
Opportunities(iii) expansion into tier-2 and tier-3 cities; (vii) diversification into grocery delivery, cloud kitchens and international markets; (xi) AI and data analytics for personalisation and efficiency
Threats(iv) intense competition from Swiggy, Blinkit and others; (viii) labour-law and food-safety regulatory changes; (xii) economic downturns reducing discretionary spending

Two TOWS strategies (use opportunities):

  • SO: Use the strong brand and loyal base (i) and the advanced technology platform (ix) to expand rapidly into tier-2 and tier-3 cities (iii), using AI and data analytics (xi) to personalise offers for new users.
  • WO: Use diversification into grocery and cloud kitchens (vii) and AI-based logistics (xi) to lift margins and overcome high operating cost and over-dependence on third-party delivery staff (ii) and the discount-driven low profitability (vi).

Draw the 2×2 SWOT and the 3×3 TOWS grid, then write the two strategies in the SO and WO cells.

2.11 The BCG (growth-share) business portfolio matrix

Asked in endsemM25 · Q2A
Start here: a simple picture

You run a family business with four shops. One old shop on the main road earns steady profit with no extra investment (it pays the family's bills). One new, trendy shop is growing fast and popular, but needs more money for stock and staff. One shop on a new road has potential but nobody knows yet if it will take off. One shop in a dying market loses money every month. You must decide where to put the family's limited money. The BCG matrix does exactly that for a company's products, classifying them by how fast the market is growing and how big a share the product has.

Definition

The Business Portfolio (Growth-Share) Matrix was developed by the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) in the 1970s. Businesses or products (Strategic Business Units, SBUs) are classified as low or high performers depending on their market growth rate and relative market share. It is among the best-known corporate portfolio analysis tools.

  • Relative market share = SBU's sales this year ÷ leading competitor's sales this year. (It shows comparative advantage through market dominance; it rests on the experience-curve idea.)
  • Market growth rate = (industry sales this year − industry sales last year) as a growth rate.
  • Why use it: to assess profiles of products, cash demands, development cycles, and resource allocation and divestment decisions.
CategoryGrowth / shareWhat the slide saysStrategy
StarsHigh / HighLeaders. Need heavy investment to maintain large share; large cash consumption and generation. Try to hold the market growth, otherwise the star becomes a cash cow. Long-term growth potential; continue substantial investment.Build / Hold
Cash cowsLow / HighFoundation of the company, often yesterday's stars. Generate more cash than required; extract profits by investing as little as possible. Mature, not growing industry. Current cash flow funds stars and question marks.Hold / Harvest
Question marksHigh / LowMost businesses start here. Absorb great cash if share stays low. Potential to become star and eventually cash cow, but can become a dog. Investment should be high.Build or Divest
DogsLow / LowCash traps with no potential to bring in much cash. Number of dogs should be minimised. Declining stage; weak position, so most analysts recommend divesting.Divest / Harvest

The product life cycle link

Steps in BCG

1
Divide the company into SBUs
→
2
Assess each SBU's relative market share and industry growth rate
→
3
Classify SBUs on the matrix
→
4
Develop strategic objectives for each SBU

Four strategies that emerge: Build / Grow, Hold / Maintain, Harvest (milk profits with minimal investment) and Divest (sell or close). Growth strategies (slide): direct expansion (increase size, revenue, operations or workforce), merger (two companies, usually of similar size, combine into a new company), acquisition (a larger company buys a smaller one and absorbs its operations).

Benefits
  • Simple and easy to understand.
  • Quickly screens opportunities.
  • Shows how corporate cash can be best used to maximise future growth and profit.
  • Corrects the one-size-fits-all target mistake: cash cows reach profit targets easily; dogs fight hopeless battles; question marks and stars starve.
Limitations
  • Only two dimensions (share and growth).
  • Data on share and growth is hard to obtain.
  • High share does not always mean profit; low share can be profitable.
  • Ignores synergy between business units.
  • Growth is not the only measure of market attractiveness.
  • No clear definition of “market”.
  • Neglects small, fast-growing competitors.
How the exam asked it

M25 · Q2A (4): “Categorise the following Nestlé products into the BCG matrix with a brief explanation of the matrix. Also create strategies for each of these Nestlé products based on the BCG matrix.” (Nescafé, Nestlé A+ plant-based curd, Milkmaid, Maggi.)

Worked answer: M25 Q2A (Nestlé)
ProductEvidence in the caseBCG classStrategy
Nescafé“dominates the instant coffee segment … ready-to-drink cold coffee gaining popularity … market still growing”StarBuild / hold: keep investing in flavours, packaging and marketing to sustain dominance.
Nestlé A+ plant-based curd alternatives“market is expanding … Nestlé is still establishing itself … competition from Epigamia and Sofit”Question markInvest selectively to gain share (distribution, promotions, product trials) or exit if share does not rise.
Milkmaid“market is shrinking … declining home-baking trends … reduce investments and focus on seasonal and niche demand”DogMinimal investment: harvest for niche and seasonal demand, divest if unprofitable. (If you stress its “strong brand nostalgia” and profitability you may argue a declining cash cow; state your reasoning either way.)
Maggi“market leader … mature market limits growth, but highly profitable”Cash cowHold and harvest: protect share with minimal investment and use the cash to fund question marks like plant-based curd.

Start with a 3-line explanation of the matrix, add the 2×2 drawing and mark the four products in the quadrants.

2.12 Porter's industry analysis and generic competitive strategies

Asked in endsemD24 · Q2AN25 · Q1CM26 · Q2A
Start here: a simple picture

Three food stalls outside the college gate. Stall A wins by being the cheapest (bulk buying, small menu, no frills). Stall B charges more but sells a unique, high-quality product everyone talks about. Stall C sells only jain-friendly rolls to the hostel and knows that small crowd perfectly. A fourth stall tries to be the cheapest and the best and serve everybody, ends up doing none well, and has no real advantage. Porter says these are the only sound ways to win: low cost, differentiation or focus; and not choosing is the trap.

Definition

Michael Porter: the fundamental basis of above-average profitability in the long run is sustainable competitive advantage. A firm can possess only two basic types of competitive advantage: low cost or differentiation. Combined with the scope of the firm's market focus, they lead to three generic strategies: overall cost leadership, differentiation and focus (the focus can be on cost or on differentiation).

StrategyWhat the firm doesSlide examples
Overall cost leadershipGains advantage by reducing cost below competitors'; watches costs closely in R&D, sales and service; can sell at low prices and still profit.Timex: simple, low-cost watches for the mass market for decades.
DifferentiationDistinguishes itself through the quality of products or services; can charge more because customers perceive extra value.Rolex (handmade gold and stainless steel, strenuous tests); Porsche; Caterpillar (prompt service and spare parts).
FocusConcentrates on a specific regional market, product line or group of buyers; either differentiation focus or cost-leadership focus within the segment.Longines sells highly jewelled watches to wealthy women; Fisher-Price makes calculators with large, bright buttons for parents of preschoolers.
Common confusion

Stuck in the middle: a company that tries to follow each generic strategy but achieves none has no competitive advantage in any industry. It competes at a disadvantage because the cost leader, the differentiators and the focusers are better positioned. (It may still earn interesting profits, but with no sustainable advantage.)

Porter's industry analysis: the five forces (supplementary, from the lesson plan)

Lecture 17 is titled “Porter's industry analysis and generic competitive strategies”. The slides cover only the generic strategies; Porter's industry analysis is the five forces model that decides how attractive an industry is: (1) threat of new entrants, (2) bargaining power of suppliers, (3) bargaining power of buyers, (4) threat of substitutes, (5) rivalry among existing competitors. The stronger the forces, the lower the profit potential. A firm then picks a generic strategy to defend itself against these forces.

How the exam asked it

D24 · Q2A (4): “Illustrate how Porter's Generic Strategy is incorporated in the cases below. Case 1: Maruti Suzuki … Case 2: Patanjali Ayurved …”
N25 · Q1C (3): “Samsung group … Analyse this case in terms of Porter's Generic strategies.”
M26 · Q2A (3): Stuck in the middle vs Blue Ocean (see 2.9).

Worked answers
  • D24 Case 1, Maruti Suzuki: Overall cost leadership. Lines: “adopts lean manufacturing and co-locates suppliers near its plants to minimise logistics expenses”; “cost-effective R&D and an extensive distribution network ensures affordable pricing without compromising quality”; “over 40% of the market share … in a highly price-sensitive market”.
  • D24 Case 2, Patanjali: Focus strategy (cost focus). Lines: “targets the niche market of health-conscious consumers seeking natural and Ayurvedic products” (narrow target), “tightly controlling its supply chain and distribution, the company kept prices competitive” (low cost within the niche).
  • N25 Q1C, Samsung: primarily differentiation. Lines: “quality, superior products and excellent customer service are considered key factors for success”; “considers defects a crime”; “digital management approach … latest technologies” (technology-led uniqueness); “leader in its field, competing against Sony” (broad target). It also avoids unrelated diversification (corporate-level focus on electronics and financial services), and attracts talent with its values. State why it is not cost leadership (no emphasis on lowest price) and not stuck in the middle (clear quality-led positioning).
End of chapter

Chapter 2: summary

  • Planning = deciding in advance what to do, how, when and by whom; it answers six questions, provides a benchmark for control, and bridges where we are and where we want to be.
  • Eight types of plans: mission → objectives → strategy → policy → procedure → rules → programmes → budgets. Policy guides thinking; procedure gives chronological steps; rule allows no flexibility. Also classified as strategic / tactical / operational, long / short term, directional / specific, single-use / standing.
  • Eight steps in planning: opportunities → objectives → premises → alternatives → compare → choose → supporting plans → budgets.
  • Objectives form a hierarchy and network, are multiple, quantitative or qualitative, and should be verifiable.
  • MBO (Drucker, 1954): objectives set jointly by superior and subordinate, reviewed periodically, linked to rewards. Benefits: participation, accountability, feedback. Weaknesses: short-run focus, inflexibility, paperwork, over-quantification.
  • Strategy has three levels (corporate, business, functional) and is developed with five tools: critical question analysis, SWOT/TOWS, Blue Ocean, BCG, Porter.
  • Blue Ocean: create uncontested market space by value innovation (low cost + differentiation) using Eliminate–Reduce–Raise–Create.
  • SWOT: internal S and W, external O and T. TOWS: SO (maxi-maxi), ST, WO, WT (mini-mini, retrenchment). The matrix changes over time; a WO move can mature into an SO strength.
  • BCG: stars (high growth, high share), cash cows (low growth, high share), question marks (high growth, low share), dogs (low, low). Strategies: build, hold, harvest, divest.
  • Porter: cost leadership, differentiation, focus; “stuck in the middle” has no advantage. Blue Ocean escapes the trade-off.

Most likely exam items: types-of-plans case (quote the lines!) · SWOT/TOWS with a company · BCG with four products · Porter cases · MBO or Blue Ocean theory.

Chapter 3

Nature of Organizing

Lectures 18-23 · structure, span, principles, departmentation, line and staff, delegation

Planning decides what to do. Organizing decides who does what, under whom, with what authority. This chapter is the most diagram-heavy in the paper: expect to draw an organisation chart (departmentation, line, or line and staff) in almost every exam. Practise sketching them quickly and neatly.

3.1 What is an organisation? Formal vs informal, tall vs flat

Start here: a simple picture

Imagine a college fest with 300 volunteers. If everyone just does whatever they feel like, you will have ten people designing posters, nobody arranging chairs, and a stage that no one is in charge of. Someone must list the jobs, group them into committees, give each committee head some power, and say who reports to whom. That act of building the “skeleton” of the event is organizing.

Definition

Organisation: a collection of people involved in pursuing defined objectives. It includes the division of work among employees and the alignment of tasks towards the ultimate goal. It is the second most important managerial function: it coordinates the work of employees, procures resources, and combines the two in pursuit of company goals.

Why organisations matter (slide): they bring together resources to achieve goals; produce goods and services efficiently; facilitate innovation; use modern manufacturing and information technology; adapt to and influence a changing environment; create value for owners, customers and employees; accommodate ongoing challenges such as diversity and ethics; and provide motivation and coordination of employees.

Formal organisation

The intentional structure of roles in a formally organised enterprise: well-defined jobs, each with a measure of authority and responsibility. It is a conscious determination by which people accomplish goals by following the norms laid down by the structure. It is designed to reach pre-determined goals, and each person answers for his or her own performance.

Informal organisation

A network of personal and social relationships not established or required by the formal organisation but arising spontaneously as people associate. It is built on likes, dislikes, feelings and emotions: friendships, the morning golf group, the weekend adventure-sports club, the coffee regulars, the bowling team. No conscious effort creates it; it emerges inside the formal set-up and has no written rules.

BasisFormal organisationInformal organisation
OriginDesigned and created by top managementComes up on its own, spontaneously
PlanningA planned oneNot planned
AuthorityFixed and defined; flows from positionBased on personal acceptance
FunctioningNeeds an office / structure to functionFunctions through people
NatureRigid, definite, with a written constitutionFlexible, no fixed written rules
Basis of relationsJobs and positionsFeelings, friendship, social ties
Remember this

Informal groups are not the enemy. They carry the grapevine, build morale and can speed up work, but they can also spread rumours and resist change. A smart manager works with the informal organisation.

Tall and flat organisations

Tall structure

Many levels of authority, narrow spans of control. Close supervision, but slow communication, higher management cost and a risk of distortion of messages.

Flat structure

Fewer levels, wide spans of control. Faster decisions and more empowered employees, but each manager is stretched and may lose control.

3.2 Nature, purpose and steps of organising

Asked in endsemN24 · Q2BD24 · Q2BJ25 · Q2BN25 · Q2BD25 · Q2B
Start here: a simple picture

Building a house: first the architect lists every job (foundation, walls, wiring, plumbing); then similar jobs are given to similar tradesmen (all electrical work to the electrician team); then each team leader is told exactly what he may decide (he can buy cables up to a limit); finally everyone knows who answers to whom. That four-part sequence is the organizing process.

Nature and purpose of organising (answer this first in every exam)

To organise means to create “a formalised, intentional internal structure of roles and positions”. For this to work the slide says there must be:

  • Verifiable objectives: people must know what the group is trying to achieve, and success must be checkable.
  • A clear idea of the major duties and activities involved in each role.
  • An understood area of discretion or authority so that the person filling the role knows what he can do to accomplish the goals.

Purpose: to divide work in a logical way, avoid duplication and gaps, fix authority and responsibility, create smooth coordination and communication, use resources efficiently, support specialisation, and make the structure flexible enough to adapt to change.

The four steps in the organising process (slide)

1
Identification of activities of the organisationlist every job that must be done to reach the objectives
→
2
Organising (grouping) the activitiesgroup similar or related activities into departments or sections (departmentation)
→
3
Classification of the authorityassign each group to a manager and give the authority needed (delegation)
→
4
Building the relationship between authority and responsibilitywho reports to whom; authority must match responsibility
StepWhat you doEveryday example (canteen)
1. Identify activitiesStudy objectives and list all tasks; leave nothing important out.Cooking, serving, billing, cleaning, buying vegetables.
2. Group the activitiesPut like activities together; this is departmentation.Kitchen team, counter team, purchase team.
3. Classify authorityAppoint a head for each group and say what he may decide.Kitchen head may order spices up to a limit.
4. Build authority-responsibility relationshipsDraw the chain of command; make responsibility equal to authority.Everyone knows the manager above and the staff below.
How the exam asked it

N24 · 2B, J25 · 2B, N25 · 2B: “Explain the nature and purpose of organizing function in management. Also discuss the steps in organizing with a suitable representation.” (3 marks).
D25 · 2B: “Explain the steps involved in organizing. Compare on four grounds between a startup and an established multinational company in terms of formal and informal structure.”
D24 · 2B (4): EcoEarth case: identify the steps taken and cite lines.

Worked answer: D24 2B (EcoEarth)
StepLine quoted from the caseExplanation
1. Identification of activities“They started by analyzing the core functions their team handles daily, from sourcing materials to customer support.”Maya and Arjun first listed all the work that had to be done and noticed overlaps and delays.
2. Organising (grouping) the activities“Priya suggested dividing tasks based on expertise … they formed dedicated teams for research and development, marketing, customer service, and logistics, each with its own supervisor.”Similar tasks were grouped into functional departments (functional departmentation) with a supervisor each.
3. Classification of authority“These supervisors would have the autonomy to make decisions within their departments but would coordinate major decisions with Maya and Arjun.”Authority was delegated to supervisors up to a limit; major decisions stayed with the founders.
4. Building authority-responsibility relationships“They worked with Priya to develop a hierarchy that balanced authority and responsibility across teams … setting clear boundaries so that every team understood its role and whom to report to.”A hierarchy (scalar chain) with clear reporting and accountability was created.
Worked answer: D25 2B (startup vs established MNC)
GroundStart-upEstablished MNC
Formal structureFew levels, loosely defined roles; founder decides; little documentation.Many levels and layers, written job descriptions, policies, rigid hierarchy and procedures.
Informal structureVery strong and closely tied to the formal one; everyone knows everyone; decisions happen over lunch or chat.Many separate informal groups across countries and functions; grapevine is large and harder to manage.
Communication and speedDirect and fast; little red tape.Mostly through the channels of the chain; slower, but more documented.
Flexibility / authorityHighly flexible; authority based on personal credibility.Authority based on position; changes need approval through levels.

Open with the four steps (with the flow figure), then the table.

3.3 Span of management (span of control)

Asked in endsemD25 · Q2C
Start here: a simple picture

A class teacher can look after 40 students in one room, but a coach can only really guide 8 batters during net practice, because each batter needs individual feedback. How many people one person can effectively supervise depends on the kind of work, not on a magic number.

Definition

Span of control is the number of subordinates who report directly to an executive or supervisor. Differences in span directly affect the shape of the organisation: narrow span → tall; wide span → flat. The optimal span is narrow enough that managers can maintain control, and wide enough that micromanaging is minimised.

The eight factors affecting span (slide)

FactorWider span possible when…Narrower span needed when…
1. Subordinates' trainingEmployees are well trained and experiencedEmployees are new or poorly trained
2. Delegation of authorityClear, adequate delegation; staff decide on their ownManager keeps most decisions; subordinates keep returning
3. PlanningClear, well-made plans and standards that people understandVague plans; manager must keep explaining
4. Rate of changeStable environment, few new situationsRapid change, frequent new problems
5. Communication techniquesGood, fast channels (IT, meetings, dashboards)Poor communication, face-to-face needed
6. Kind of activitySimple, repetitive, similar jobsComplex, varied, creative jobs
7. Kind of organisationSubordinates work close together in one placeDispersed, many locations
8. Organisation levelLower levels (routine work): 10-20 or moreTop level (complex decisions): about 4-8

Graicunas' relationship formula (enrichment, shows why span is limited)

V. A. Graicunas pointed out that adding a subordinate adds many more relationships than one. For a manager with n subordinates, the number of possible relationships (direct single, cross and direct group) is

R = n [ 2n−1 + (n − 1) ]

n2345678
R618441002224901080

Check n = 4: 4 [ 23 + 3 ] = 4 × 11 = 44. The relationships grow far faster than the head-count, which is why a manager cannot supervise too many people closely.

How the exam asked it

D25 · 2C (3): “As the HR manager of a mid-sized manufacturing company, determine an appropriate span of control for the production managers using the four factors. Explain how you would apply these factors to decide the number of direct reports for each manager to ensure effective supervision and minimize micromanagement.”

Worked answer

Choose four factors and tie each to the production floor; then give a number.

  • Training of subordinates: operators are trained and certified on machines → each manager can handle more people; for newly hired trainees reduce the span.
  • Kind of activity: assembly and machining are routine and repetitive, with standard operating procedures → wide span possible.
  • Delegation of authority: shift supervisors can stop the line for quality and approve minor repairs → fewer escalations, which allows a wider span.
  • Communication techniques: digital production boards, daily stand-up meetings and a shop-floor messaging group allow quick contact → wider span.

Decision: a span of about 8-10 direct reports for production managers (supervisors, who themselves lead 15-20 operators). Review the number when the product mix or the workforce changes. A span this size avoids micromanagement (managers cannot hover over everyone) yet keeps control (a manageable number of reports).

3.4 Urwick's ten principles of organising

Asked in endsemM25 · Q2BM26 · Q2BJ26 · Q2B
Start here: a simple picture

Think of a well-run railway: one clear destination, each train has one driver, rules say who may give signals, and the timetable changes if a track is closed. These everyday common-sense rules of running a railway are what Urwick wrote down as principles for running any organisation.

Lyndall F. Urwick (1891-1983) was a British management consultant who combined the ideas of earlier thinkers such as Henri Fayol into a comprehensive theory of administration. His influential book is The Elements of Business Administration (1943).

#PrincipleMeaning (slide)Keyword clue in a case
1Unity of objectivesThe structure is effective if it enables individuals to contribute to enterprise objectives. A common goal for the whole business; without it departments set conflicting goals.“aligned goals with the company's vision”, “common direction”
2Organisational efficiencyThe structure aids accomplishment of objectives with a minimum of unsought consequences or costs.“eliminated redundant steps”, “optimal use of resources”, “without increasing costs”
3SpecialisationThe whole work is divided among subordinates on the basis of qualifications, abilities and skills.“assigned tasks based on expertise”, “each focused on what they were skilled at”
4Span of managementThe number of persons an individual can manage effectively is limited; the exact number depends on underlying variables.“limited number of employees per manager”, “balanced span”
5Scalar chainA chain of command flowing from upper to lowest levels; clarifies who reports to whom.“clear line of reporting from top to bottom”
6Unity of commandEvery subordinate is answerable and accountable to one boss at one time.“instructions from only one supervisor”, “no conflicting orders”
7DelegationAuthority must be delegated as far down as possible; adequate authority so people can accomplish expected results.“entrusted decisions to team leaders”, “empowered”
8Parity of authority and responsibilityResponsibility cannot be greater than the authority delegated, nor less. Subordinates' responsibility to superiors is absolute; superiors cannot escape responsibility for their subordinates' activities.“authority along with responsibility”, “balanced”, “accountable”
9FlexibilityStructure must be simple to understand and adaptable to changes in the nature of business, technology and procedures.“adapt quickly to market changes”, “dynamic framework”
10Functional definitionEvery position and department must have a clear definition of results expected, activities to be undertaken and authority delegated.“clearly outlined roles”, “defined responsibilities”
Common confusion

Be careful with look-alikes. Delegation (giving authority down) vs parity (authority equals responsibility) vs scalar chain (the line of reporting) vs functional definition (clear roles). If a case says “assigned authority with clear responsibilities”, name Delegation first and mention Parity as the second principle, then justify.

How the exam asked it

M25 · 2B, M26 · 2B, J26 · 2B (3 marks each): Three short cases, “identify the Urwick's principles … and explain them in brief”. Each part is worth 1 mark: name + one-line link to the case.

Worked answers (all three papers)

M25 2B

  • (i) Vikram entrusted key decisions to team leaders, kept overall accountability → Principle of Delegation (authority passed down as far as possible) together with Parity of authority and responsibility (“assigning authority with clear responsibilities”).
  • (ii) Priya assigned tasks according to expertise → Principle of Specialisation: work divided according to skills and abilities, reducing errors and raising productivity.
  • (iii) Rohan aligned all departments to the company's vision → Principle of Unity of Objectives: one common aim prevents conflicting departmental goals.

M26 2B

  • (i) Neha: each manager oversaw a limited number of employees → Span of Management: balanced span gives better communication and coordination.
  • (ii) Arjun: each employee received instructions from only one supervisor → Unity of Command: one boss at a time removes conflicting orders.
  • (iii) Ravi: gave project leaders authority along with responsibility → Parity of Authority and Responsibility: neither more nor less than the other.

J26 2B

  • (i) Meera: eliminated redundant steps, optimised resources, no extra cost → Organisational Efficiency: objectives achieved with a minimum of unsought costs.
  • (ii) Rajesh: dynamic framework adapting to market changes without disrupting operations → Flexibility: structure adaptable to changes in business and technology.
  • (iii) Kavita: clearly outlined roles and reporting structures → Functional Definition (clear roles, results and authority); the reporting lines also reflect the Scalar Chain.

3.5 Departmentation: grouping activities

Asked in endsemN24 · Q2CD24 · Q2CM25 · Q2CJ25 · Q2CN25 · Q2CM26 · Q2CJ26 · Q2C
Start here: a simple picture

A school has hundreds of tasks. It could group teachers by subject (maths dept, science dept) or by class (primary, secondary) or by campus (city branch, suburban branch) or by shift (morning, afternoon). Each is a way of departmentation. There is no single right way; each school chooses what fits, and large organisations mix several.

Definition

Departmentation is the process of dividing the whole work into a number of jobs (so that no important activity is left out), then bringing together homogeneous jobs into groups and deciding their relation to each other. It involves many decisions about a logical division of work and leads to the establishment of a number of manageable units.

The eight patterns (slide)

  1. Simple numbers · 2. Time · 3. Enterprise functions · 4. Territory / geography · 5. Product · 6. Process / equipment · 7. Customer · 8. Matrix
1. By simple numbers

Group people who perform the same duties under one manager (for example 50 labourers under one supervisor). An age-old method, now falling into disuse because technology demands specialised skills, and groups of specialists are more efficient than groups built only on numbers. Useful only at the lowest level.

2. By time (shift)

The oldest form; suited to lower levels. Used where the work is continuous, e.g. hospitals and production plants.

Advantages
  • Services offered 24 x 7 instead of 8 hours.
  • Continuous processes are not interrupted.
  • Expensive capital equipment used for more than 8 hours a day.
  • Students can work at night shifts to sustain their living.
Limitations
  • Supervision during the night shift is difficult.
  • Fatigue: hard for employees to change their biological clock.
  • Several shifts cause coordination and communication problems.
  • Overtime payment raises cost.
3. By enterprise function

The most widely used form. Activities that are alike are placed together in one department under a single chain of command (production, marketing, finance, HR). It is consistent with specialisation and division of work, and makes coordination easier since one supervisor is in charge of one major area.

Strengths
  • Economies of scale within functional departments.
  • In-depth knowledge and skill development.
  • Helps accomplish functional goals.
  • Best with only one or a few products.
Weaknesses
  • Slow response to environmental change.
  • Decisions pile on top; hierarchy overload.
  • Poor horizontal coordination between departments.
  • Less innovation; restricted view of organisational goals.
4. By territory / geography

Group activities by territory, useful when customers are geographically dispersed. Slide example: Coca-Cola has two broad geographic areas, North America and the international sector (Pacific Rim, Europe, Africa and Latin America).

Advantages
  • Places responsibility at the lower levels.
  • Emphasis on local markets and local problems.
  • Improves co-ordination within a region.
  • Takes advantage of economies of local operation.
  • Better face-to-face communication with local interests.
  • Measurable training ground for general managers.
Limitations
  • Requires more persons with general manager abilities.
  • Makes maintenance of economical central services difficult.
  • Increases the problem of top management control.
  • Possible duplication of functions in each region.
5. By product (or service)

Each product or service line becomes a division. Useful in services too: a food company may have frozen-food, dairy-products and produce departments.

Advantages
  • Focus and expertise on each product.
  • Profit and performance can be measured per product.
  • Quick response to product-market changes.
  • Trains general managers.
Limitations
  • Duplication of functions and higher cost.
  • Coordination difficulty between divisions.
  • Competition for corporate resources.
6. By process or equipment

Activities are grouped around a stage of the production process or a type of machine (cutting, machining, painting; or computer centre, X-ray unit). Good when expensive equipment or specialised skills are needed, and for sequential production.

Merits: economies from fully used equipment, specialised skills, ease of training. Limits: poor coordination between process units, inflexible to product changes, responsibility for the final product is spread out.

7. By customer

Group activities by common customers or types of customers, on the assumption that customers in each department have a common set of problems and needs best met by specialists. Examples: retail, corporate and government banking; adult and children's wards; wholesale and retail divisions.

Advantages
  • Services and products tailored to each group's needs.
  • Specialist knowledge of the customer; stronger loyalty.
  • Faster, more responsive service.
  • Accountability for each customer segment.
Challenges
  • Duplication of staff and facilities.
  • Coordination between customer units is harder.
  • If one segment shrinks, resources lie idle.
  • Conflict over priorities and shared resources.
8. Matrix (project) departmentation
Start here: a simple picture

A film unit. A cinematographer belongs to the camera department (his home function) but is also on loan to the movie “Project X”, reporting to its director for the film's duration. He has two bosses: the head of the camera department and the project director.

Definition

A matrix structure superimposes a horizontal set of divisional (project/product) reporting relationships onto a hierarchical functional structure. Its essence is the combination of functional and product or project patterns in the same structure.

Pros
  • Flexible use of scarce experts across projects.
  • Combines functional depth with project focus.
  • Good communication and teamwork between specialists.
  • Quick response to changing project needs.
Cons
  • Dual command violates unity of command: confusion, role conflict.
  • Power struggles between functional and project managers.
  • Complex; needs many meetings and good interpersonal skills.
  • Higher administrative cost.

Choosing the basis

Use function for a small firm with few products; territory for spread-out markets; product for many diverse products; customer for distinct buyer groups; time for 24-hour operations; process for technical production; matrix for project work. Large organisations combine several, which is the hybrid approach asked in M26 and J26.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 2C, J25 · 2C, N25 · 2C (3 marks, three papers): “Propose a scheme of departmentation for an MNC with a field network of sales all over the country. Discuss its merits and limitations.”
D24 · 2C: customer departmentalization (with chart, advantages and challenges).
M25 · 2C: a description (construction, aerospace, advertising campaign, EDP installation, consulting firms) → identify the structure.
M26 · 2C (4): “Design an organizational structure for a multinational company using appropriate departmentation methods.”
J26 · 2C: healthcare organisation, “departmentation strategy integrating multiple approaches”.

Worked answer: N24 / J25 / N25 2C (MNC with country-wide sales network)

Scheme: functional departmentation at the top (production, finance, HR, marketing and sales), and territorial (geographic) departmentation inside Marketing & Sales: North, South, East, West zones, each with area / branch field offices.

Merits
  • Local managers know local markets and customers; quick decisions.
  • Responsibility is placed at lower levels; trains general managers.
  • Better face-to-face contact and regional coordination.
  • Functional departments keep specialist depth at HQ.
Limitations
  • Needs many managers with general-management ability.
  • Duplication of functions across zones raises cost.
  • Top management control and central services become harder.
  • Risk of zones pursuing local goals against company goals.
Worked answer: M25 2C (the matrix clue)

The description (bridge construction, satellite design, advertising campaign, data-processing installation, consulting teams with experts from different fields) is matrix (project) departmentation. Draw the grid: functions (engineering, finance, marketing) as columns, projects as rows, with specialists at the intersections reporting to a functional head and a project manager. Give the pros and cons above, ending with the dual-command problem.

Worked answer: M26 2C (multinational, several methods)

Use geography at the top (regions), product inside each region, and functions as shared staff at HQ.

Why: regional heads understand local markets; product divisions keep product focus; corporate staff avoid duplicating finance, HR, legal and R&D in every region. Close with one limitation (cost of duplication in each region) and how it is reduced (shared services).

Worked answer: J26 2C (healthcare)
  • Service/product: clinical departments (cardiology, orthopaedics, paediatrics) → specialised expertise.
  • Customer: emergency, OPD and inpatient units → each patient group gets tailored workflows, improving patient care.
  • Time: nursing in three shifts → round-the-clock care.
  • Function: pharmacy, laboratory, finance and HR as support → efficiency and cost control.

Link back to the question: patient care improves through specialisation and tailored units; operational efficiency improves through shared support services and shift cover.

Worked answer: D24 2C (customer departmentalization)

Draw the bank chart above. Explain: a customer-focused unit builds specialist knowledge (for example, corporate bankers who understand working-capital needs), allows tailored products and faster response, and raises loyalty. Challenges: duplicated staff and branches, coordination between units, idle capacity if a segment shrinks, and conflict over shared resources.

3.6 Line, staff and functional authority: line and line-and-staff organisation

Asked in endsemD24 · Q3AM25 · Q3AJ25 · Q3AN25 · Q3AD25 · Q3AJ26 · Q3A
Start here: a simple picture

In an army, the commanding officer and his battalion commanders give orders and fight; that is line. The army also has intelligence analysts, engineers and legal advisers who study problems and advise the commander but never command his soldiers; that is staff. Line decides and orders; staff advises and supports.

Authority and responsibility (slide)

Authority is the right to give orders: the rightful legal power to request subordinates to do certain things or refrain from doing so, with the manager able, if need be, to take disciplinary action or even discharge the subordinate. Responsibility means obligation, liability, activity or accountability: the obligation of a subordinate, to whom a supervisor has assigned a task, to perform the service required.

Line organisation

Definition

The oldest type of organisation, also called military, vertical or scalar organisation. Persons with greater decision-making authority are at the top, those with the least at the bottom, with intermediate or supervisory levels between.

Four features to quote in an exam (slide):

  1. Simplest form of organisation: easy to understand and set up.
  2. Line of authority flows from top to bottom: a single scalar chain; orders go down, accountability goes up.
  3. Unified control by the line officers: they can take decisions independently in their own area, which brings efficiency in communication and stability to the concern.
  4. No specialised and supportive services: there are no staff specialists; line managers do everything themselves.
Merits
  • Simple, economical, clear authority.
  • Quick decisions; unity of command.
  • Easy to fix responsibility; good discipline.
Demerits
  • Overload on line managers; no specialist advice.
  • Rigid, communication only through the chain, slow in large firms.
  • Over-dependence on a few key people.

Line and staff organisation

Definition

A line and staff organisation is one where specialist advisers in the form of functional managers assist the line managers in performing their responsibilities. The power of command always remains with the line executives; staff supervisors guide, advise and counsel the line executives. Line and staff functions frequently overlap, and most staff executives may simultaneously be line and functional executives.

Two types of staff (slide): Staff assistants, such as the PA to the Managing Director or the Secretary to the Marketing Manager; and staff supervisors / specialists, such as the Operation Control Manager or the Quality Controller.

Four features to quote (slide):

  1. A compromise of line organisation, more complex than a pure line concern.
  2. Division of work and specialisation take place.
  3. The whole organisation is divided into functional areas to which staff specialists are attached.
  4. Efficiency through specialisation: command stays with the line executive and staff serves only as counsellors.
BasisLineStaff
RoleDirectly achieves the objectives (production, sales)Supports and advises (HR, legal, quality, R&D)
AuthorityCommand authority; can give ordersAdvisory only (right to advise, recommend)
ChainPart of the scalar chainOutside the direct chain
AccountabilityFor resultsFor quality of advice

Functional staff authority (supplementary)

Lecture 21 names “line, staff and functional staff authority”. Functional authority is a limited right delegated to a staff specialist to command in a specific area across departments, for example the Quality Controller may insist that every plant follows a particular inspection procedure, or the HR head may require all managers to follow the appraisal policy. It deliberately cuts across unity of command, so it is kept narrow.

Common confusion

How to avoid line-staff conflict (asked in D25 3A: “without creating conflicts of authority”): define roles clearly in writing; staff must sell ideas, not order; line must consult staff and give them access to facts; keep staff accountable for the results of their advice; use functional authority only in narrow areas; hold joint meetings.

How the exam asked it

M25 · 3A: four features of line organisation with a block diagram of an FMCG start-up. N25 · 3A and J26 · 3A: a steel-bolt company adopting a line structure: how authority, communication and decision-making work, and draw the chart. J25 · 3A: four features of line and staff with a multi-specialty hospital diagram. D25 · 3A: automobile firm with line and staff: how roles operate without conflict, and draw a chart. D24 · 3A: draw a line-and-staff chart for a company of your choice, describe contributions and give collaboration situations.

Worked answer: N25 / J26 3A (steel bolts, line structure)
  • Authority: flows in a single line from the owner to production, sales and purchase managers, then to supervisors and workers. Each person has one boss (unity of command).
  • Communication: vertical, through the chain: orders go down, reports go up. Short chain in a small firm, so it is quick and clear.
  • Decision-making: centralised at the top for policy (pricing, investments); line managers decide independently in their own sections (the foreman decides machine allocation). Fast, because there is no committee or staff approval.
  • Efficiency: clear accountability (if bolts fail the quality check, the foreman answers); low overhead since there are no specialist staff.

Draw the line chart above (owner → managers → supervisors → workers).

Worked answer: M25 3A (FMCG start-up, four features)

Use the four features in the box above and tie each to the chart: (1) simple: founder with only three heads; (2) authority top to bottom: head → area sales lead → field team; (3) unified control: each head independently controls his function so decisions in a growing start-up are fast; (4) no specialists: no separate legal or quality staff, so the heads handle it themselves, which keeps costs low. Mention that as the start-up grows it will add staff specialists.

Worked answer: J25 3A (hospital) and D25 3A (automobile)

Hospital: (1) line and staff is a compromise that is more complex than line: the Medical Director commands chiefs of surgery, medicine and nursing; (2) specialisation: clinical, nursing and support work are divided; (3) staff specialists attached to functional areas: quality control, legal, HR, IT and records advise the director; (4) command stays with line: staff do not instruct surgeons but counsel, for example the quality controller recommends infection-control protocols and the line chief adopts them.

Automobile: line executives (VPs of manufacturing, sales and operations) own production and sales decisions; staff specialists (R&D, quality control, legal, HR, finance) advise. To avoid conflict: written role descriptions; staff advise but do not command; limited functional authority for quality standards; line must consult staff before major technical decisions; shared goals and joint reviews.

Worked answer: D24 3A (company of your choice)

Choose a company (for example a hospital or car maker, use the chart above). Describe how each line function contributes (production makes the product, sales earns revenue) and how each staff function contributes (quality control reduces defects; HR provides trained people; legal limits risk). Collaboration example: a rise in warranty claims is solved by production (line), quality control (staff) and R&D (staff) jointly finding the defect, redesigning the part and retraining workers.

3.7 Delegation of authority

Asked in endsemN24 · Q3AM26 · Q3A
Start here: a simple picture

The head cook gives a junior cook the job of preparing the gravy for tonight's banquet, tells him the taste and quantity expected, lets him choose spices and use the pantry, and will ask him how it went afterwards. If the gravy fails, the head cook still faces the host, but the junior is also answerable. That is delegation: result expected, task given, authority given, obligation created.

Definition

Delegation: the entire process of delegation involves the determination of results expected, the assignment of tasks, and the delegation of authority for accomplishment of these tasks.

The four steps in the process of delegation (slide: “Flow of Delegation”)

1
Determination of results expectedfrom persons in a position
→
2
Assignment of tasksto persons in a position
→
3
Delegation of authorityfor accomplishing these tasks
→
4
Creating the obligationfor the subordinate to perform the duties assigned
StepMeaningKey point
1. Determine results expectedState clearly what outcome, standard and deadline are required.Delegate results, not just activities.
2. Assign tasksGive specific tasks to a capable person.Match task to skill and workload.
3. Delegate authorityGive the right to make decisions and use resources needed to do the task.Authority must be adequate (parity principle).
4. Create obligationThe subordinate accepts the duty to perform and report; becomes accountable.The manager keeps ultimate responsibility.

Authority, responsibility and accountability

  • Authority flows down and can be delegated.
  • Responsibility is the duty to perform; the subordinate's obligation is created at delegation.
  • Accountability flows up; the superior can never escape it (Urwick: “absolute” responsibility to the superior).

Principles and benefits (supplementary standard points)

  • Principles: delegate results expected; authority matches responsibility; unity of command; delegate as far down as possible; clear communication of limits; control and feedback after delegation.
  • Benefits: relieves managers for higher-level work; develops subordinates; faster decisions; motivation.
  • Barriers: fear of losing control, lack of trust, unwillingness of subordinates to accept responsibility, poor communication.
How the exam asked it

N24 · 3A (3): a new team leader trains an employee to handle customer escalations independently: “Following the Flow of Delegation model, analyze how the team leader would apply each step.”
M26 · 3A (3): “Explain the four steps in the process of delegation with a suitable example.”

Worked answer: N24 3A (customer escalations)
  • 1. Results expected: resolve level-2 escalations within 24 hours with at least 90% customer satisfaction and without repeated callbacks.
  • 2. Assign tasks: the employee takes escalated calls, logs the case in the CRM, investigates and calls the customer back; first shadowing, then handling independently.
  • 3. Delegate authority: allow him to offer refunds or goodwill credits up to a stated limit, access billing records, and coordinate with the technical team without asking permission each time.
  • 4. Create obligation: he accepts accountability for outcomes, reports daily on open cases and unresolved issues; the team leader stays ultimately responsible to management and gives feedback.
Worked answer: M26 3A (any suitable example)

Example: a store manager delegates monthly inventory reconciliation to an assistant manager. (1) Result: stock records match physical stock within 1% by the 5th of each month. (2) Task: count, compare with system records, investigate differences. (3) Authority: access to inventory software, ability to instruct the storekeepers and approve small write-offs. (4) Obligation: the assistant promises to deliver the reconciled report, and answers for it; the store manager remains accountable to the regional head.

End of chapter

Chapter 3: summary

  • Organising creates a formalised, intentional structure of roles. Needs verifiable objectives, clear duties and an understood area of authority. Four steps: identify activities → group them → classify authority → build authority-responsibility relationships.
  • Formal organisation is planned, position-based and rigid; informal is spontaneous, people-based and flexible. Tall = many levels, narrow span; flat = few levels, wide span.
  • Span of control is affected by eight factors: subordinates' training, delegation, planning, rate of change, communication, kind of activity, kind of organisation, level. Graicunas: R = n[2n−1 + (n − 1)].
  • Urwick's ten principles: unity of objectives, organisational efficiency, specialisation, span, scalar chain, unity of command, delegation, parity of authority and responsibility, flexibility, functional definition.
  • Departmentation has eight patterns: numbers, time, function, territory, product, process/equipment, customer, matrix. Large firms use hybrids. Matrix has dual command.
  • Line organisation: simplest, authority top to bottom, unified control, no specialists. Line and staff: specialists advise, command stays with line; compromise, specialisation. Functional authority is a narrow exception.
  • Authority is the right to command; responsibility the obligation to perform; they must be equal. Delegation = results expected → tasks → authority → obligation.

Most likely exam items: departmentation scheme with chart (appeared in 7 of 8 papers) · line / line-and-staff chart · Urwick cases · steps in organising · delegation steps.

Chapter 4

Talent Acquisition and Management

Lectures 24-28 · HRM and HRD, job analysis, recruitment, selection, training, induction, systems approach to staffing

Staffing is the part of managing that fills and keeps filled the positions in the structure that Chapter 3 designed. This chapter is full of lists, processes and company examples. Most questions are application questions (“you are the HR manager of …”), so learn each list and be ready to attach a company example to it.

4.1 HRM, HRD and the benefits of integrating them

Asked in endsemN24 · Q3BD25 · Q3BM26 · Q3B
Start here: a simple picture

A hospital has two kinds of work. One team keeps the hospital running every day: admits patients, keeps records, pays salaries, enforces rules (that is like HRM). Another team trains doctors in new surgical techniques and prepares nurses for promotion (that is like HRD). A hospital needs both: running the present and growing the future.

Definition

HRM (Human Resource Management) focuses on managing people within an organisation: administrative tasks, policies and procedures. HRD (Human Resource Development) emphasises enhancing employees' skills, knowledge and capabilities for growth and organisational success through learning and development.

HRM is the bigger concept; HRD is a part of it. HRM covers planning, staffing, developing, monitoring, maintaining, managing relationships and evaluating. HRD covers the development part: training, learning, career development, talent management, performance appraisal, employee engagement and empowerment.

BasisHRMHRD
FocusManaging people and administrationDeveloping people's skills and potential
ScopeWider: all people-related functionsNarrower: a sub-set concerned with development
Time viewPresent needs: day to dayFuture needs: long term growth
NatureMostly administrative and operationalMostly developmental and learning-oriented
Typical activitiesJob analysis, HR planning, recruitment, selection, placement, induction and orientationTraining and development, career development, organisational development

Functions of HRM (slide): managerial functions: planning, organising, directing, controlling; operative functions: job analysis, HR planning, recruitment, selection, placement, induction and orientation. Functions of HRD: training and development, career development, organisational development.

Benefits of integrating HRM and HRD (slide)

1. Holistic employee development

A comprehensive approach to immediate support and long-term skill enhancement.

2. Strategic alignment

HR practices align directly with organisational goals, enhancing strategic objectives.

3. Improved productivity

Well-rounded development boosts skills and engagement, leading to higher efficiency.

4. Enhanced talent retention

Investing in development builds loyalty and reduces turnover.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 3B (3): differences between HRM and HRD and how they complement each other for long-term success. D25 · 3B (3): as HR manager of a mid-sized IT company, apply the benefits of integrating HRM and HRD to design a strategy for productivity and retention. M26 · 3B (3): any three benefits of integrating with a suitable example for each.

Worked answer: D25 3B (IT company strategy) and M26 3B (three benefits with examples)
  • Holistic development: an IT firm onboards a fresher (HRM: induction, payroll, policies) and immediately places the same person in a six-month cloud-skills programme (HRD) → a rounded employee from day one.
  • Strategic alignment: if the company's strategy is to move into AI services, HRM hires data-science talent and HRD upskills existing developers in machine learning → people capability follows the strategy.
  • Improved productivity: continuous learning plus clear job roles reduce errors and idle time; developers certified on a new stack deliver faster.
  • Retention: career paths, mentoring and sponsored certifications make employees stay; lower attrition reduces hiring cost (Amazon's Career Choice funding tuition is a real example).

For “design a strategy”, structure it as: onboarding → skill-gap analysis → targeted training → appraisal linked to career path → recognition, and name the metric (attrition rate, productivity per engineer).

4.2 Job analysis, job description and job specification

Asked in endsemD24 · Q3BJ25 · Q3BN25 · Q3BJ26 · Q3B
Start here: a simple picture

Before posting a vacancy for a “cook” at a hostel mess, you must answer: What will he actually do all day? (job description) and What kind of person can do it? (job specification). Without that, you may hire a person who can make wonderful desserts for a job that needs cooking for 500 people at 6 a.m.

  • Job: a group of tasks that must be performed for an organisation to achieve its goals.
  • Position: a collection of tasks and responsibilities performed by one person; there is a position for every individual.
  • Job analysis: the systematic process of determining the skills, duties and knowledge required for performing jobs. It answers: what skills are needed? what qualification? what desirable abilities? what work experience? what responsibilities?
  • Job description: a document giving information on the tasks, duties and responsibilities of a job (the job).
  • Job specification: the minimum qualifications (knowledge, skills, abilities, experience, personal traits) needed to perform the job (the person).

Job analysis (tasks, responsibilities, duties; knowledge, skills, abilities) leads to job descriptions and job specifications, which feed HR planning, recruitment, selection, training and development, performance appraisal, compensation and benefits, safety and health, employee and labour relations, and legal compliance.

Job descriptionJob specification
DescribesThe jobThe person required
ContainsTitle, reporting line, purpose, duties, responsibilities, working conditionsEducation, experience, skills, abilities, personal attributes, physical demands
Used forAdvertising, orientation, appraisalScreening and selection
How the exam asked it

D24 · 3B: JD and JS for a Graduate Engineer Trainee in an R&D department. J25 · 3B and J26 · 3B: JD and JS for an entry-level fresher position in your own domain. N25 · 3B: a job specification on 6 factors for a Nestlé Graduate Engineer Trainee reporting to the Production & Maintenance Manager (Technical), Bengaluru factory.

Model answer: JD and JS for a Graduate Engineer Trainee (R&D)

Job description

Job titleGraduate Engineer Trainee (GET), R&D Department
Reports toSenior Manager, Research and Development

PurposeSupport design, testing and improvement of new products under supervision
DutiesAssist in prototyping and experiments; collect and analyse test data; prepare technical reports; maintain lab records; support patent and literature search
ResponsibilitiesAccuracy of data, adherence to safety rules, timely progress reports

Job specification (the six factors)

2. ExperienceFresher; internship or project work in the area is an advantage
3. Technical knowledge and skillsCore subject fundamentals; data analysis tools; CAD or simulation software; Excel/Python
4. Abilities / aptitudeAnalytical and problem-solving ability; numerical and verbal ability; learning agility
5. Personality traitsCuriosity, teamwork, integrity, emotional stability, initiative
6. Physical and special requirementsFit for lab work; willing to travel and work shifts; fluent English
Model answer: Nestlé GET (Production & Maintenance, Bengaluru) specification

Education: B.E./B.Tech in Mechanical, Electrical, Chemical or Food Technology. Experience: fresher; internship in a manufacturing or FMCG plant preferred. Skills: knowledge of plant machinery, maintenance practices, safety and quality standards (HACCP, GMP), basic automation, Excel/ERP. Abilities: analytical thinking, troubleshooting, ability to read technical drawings. Personality: discipline, teamwork, shop-floor leadership, adaptability to shifts. 4.3 Recruitment: process, types, sources and challenges

Asked in endsemN24 · Q4AD24 · Q4AM25 · Q3BM25 · Q4AJ25 · Q4AN25 · Q4AM26 · Q4AJ26 · Q4A
Start here: a simple picture

A cricket academy needs a new wicket-keeper. First it decides it needs one (hiring need), writes what he must do (job description), then spreads the word (district trials, club scouts, social media). Recruitment is the search and invitation stage: it creates a pool of interested people. Selection, the next stage, picks one from that pool.

Definition

Recruitment is the process of locating, identifying and attracting capable candidates, for current or future needs. It is the search for prospective employees to suit the job requirements as represented by the job specification. Selection picks the right person from among them; placement puts the selected person on the job most suited to him.

The 10-step recruitment process (slide)

1
Identifying hiring needsvacancy or new role; approved headcount

3
Sourcing candidatesinternal and external channels

4

→
6
