→
7
Background checksreferences, education, employment
→
8
Decision makingpick the best, keep a runner-up
→
9
Offer and negotiationsalary, role, joining date
→
10
Onboardinginduction into the organisation
How the exam asked it

D24 · 4A and M25 · 4A (3): “Describe the 10-step recruitment process for finding the right candidate for a job.”

How to write it in the exam

List all ten steps in order with one line each (what happens and why), and if time permits tie them to a short example, e.g. a software company hiring a data analyst. Draw the flow in a vertical column.

Types of recruitment (slide)

Internal

Hiring from within the organisation to fill a vacancy.

External

Sourcing candidates from outside.

Campus

Recruiting fresh graduates directly from universities.

Executive search

Specialised hiring of senior executives ("headhunting").

Contingent

Agencies are paid only if they fill the position.

Remote

Hiring for work outside a traditional office.

Diversity and inclusion

Strategies for a diverse, inclusive workforce.

Referral

Candidates recommended by employees or networks.

Social media

LinkedIn, Twitter, Facebook to attract candidates.

Full cycle

All stages from sourcing to onboarding handled together.

Digital

Online portals, applicant-tracking systems, AI screening.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 4A (3): “Evaluate three types of recruitment methods commonly used by modern businesses. For each method, provide examples and assess how it aligns with organisational goals and talent needs.”

Worked answer: N24 4A
  • Campus recruitment: TCS and Infosys hire large batches of freshers from engineering colleges. Aligns with scale-up goals and long-term talent pipeline; cost-efficient and trainable; limitation: no experience.
  • Referral recruitment: Employees recommend friends; quick, cheaper, better cultural fit and retention; aligns with goals of fast hiring of reliable people; limitation: may reduce diversity.
  • Social media / digital recruitment: LinkedIn campaigns for niche skills; wide reach, fast, good for employer branding; aligns with the need for specialised, tech-savvy talent; limitation: high volume of applications to screen.

Sources of recruitment (slide)

1. Internal sources
  • Promotion
  • Transfer
  • Demotion
  • Retired employees (re-employment)
  • Notice boards / job posting
2. External sources
  • Press advertisements
  • Educational institutes (campus)
  • Placement agencies
  • Employment agencies / exchanges
  • Unsolicited applicants (walk-ins)
  • Employee recommendation
Internal: advantages
  • Motivates employees: visible career growth.
  • Cheaper and faster; no extra advertising.
  • Known performance; lower risk of a wrong hire.
  • Shorter induction; knows the culture; loyalty.
Internal: limits
  • No fresh ideas; limited pool.
  • Possible jealousy among those not chosen.
  • Creates another vacancy lower down.
External: advantages
  • New ideas, skills and perspectives.
  • Large talent pool; may bring competitor knowledge.
  • Suitable for new, specialised posts.
External: limits
  • Costly and slow; more screening.
  • Uncertainty about fit; longer induction.
  • May demotivate existing employees.
How the exam asked it

M25 · 3B: FMCG company promotes an experienced team member to team leader: why is internal recruitment beneficial? N25 · 4A, J26 · 4A: as CHRO of Tata Motors pick 3 internal and 3 external sources and justify to the Board. M26 · 4A: recommend 3 internal and 3 external sources for AB Corporation, a mid-sized manufacturer.

Worked answers

M25 3B: The post must be filled quickly and an internal promotion is fastest: the candidate is already known (performance record available), needs minimal induction because he knows products, processes and culture, costs nothing in advertising, and motivates the whole team by showing that growth is possible; it also builds loyalty and reduces attrition.

N25 / J26 (Tata Motors): Internal: (1) promotion of experienced engineers to supervisory grades: rewards performance, retains knowledge; (2) transfer between plants (Pune, Jamshedpur, Sanand): fills gaps without hiring, develops multi-plant skills; (3) job posting / notice board within the group (Tata Motors, JLR, Tata Technologies): transparent, quick. External: (1) campus recruitment from engineering colleges: fresh engineers for EV and software roles; (2) executive search for senior R&D and electric-vehicle leadership; (3) social media / digital (LinkedIn): niche talent in AI, battery and embedded systems.

M26 (AB Corporation): Internal: promotion, transfer, retired-employee re-engagement for skilled machinists. External: campus recruitment (ITI and diploma institutes), employee referrals, placement agencies for temporary or bulk hiring. Justify each with cost, speed and fit.

Challenges in recruitment (slide)

Talent shortage · high competition · time and resource constraints · evolving job market and skills gap · diversity and inclusion · candidate experience · technology and automation · compliance and regulations · retention and turnover · market and industry dynamics.

How the exam asked it

J25 · 4A (3): “As a Talent Acquisition Manager … identify three major challenges and explain how you would address each to ensure an effective and inclusive hiring process.”

Worked answer
  • Talent shortage / skills gap: build a pipeline through campus tie-ups, internships, reskilling existing staff and employer branding.
  • Diversity and inclusion: write unbiased job ads, use diverse interview panels and structured interviews, blind screening of CVs, sourcing from varied channels and women-returnship programmes.
  • Candidate experience: a quick, transparent process with timely feedback, a simple application portal, and respectful communication; avoid long delays that lose good candidates (also addresses high competition).

4.4 Selection: procedure, tests and interviews

Asked in endsemJ25 · Q4BD25 · Q4A
Start here: a simple picture

Recruitment is like casting a wide net; selection is picking the fish you want. You check the photo (application), ask a quick question (preliminary interview), take a test, ask deeper questions (interview), call a few people who know the candidate (references) and then decide.

Definition

Selection refers to picking from among the candidates the one that best meets the position requirements.

Steps in the selection procedure (slide, six steps)

1
Initial / preliminary interviewbasic qualifications and fit
→
2
Application formfactual record: education, experience, expected pay
→
3
Reference checksformer employers and unrelated referees
→
4
Employment testsmeasure qualities against job specification
→
5
Interviewcore, in-depth assessment
→
6
Selection decisionbest fit chosen, runner-up kept in reserve
  • Application form: provides factual information to evaluate suitability; later part of employee record. Contains identifying information, education, experience, expected salary, allowances and benefits, community activities.
  • Reference checks: the applicant names former employers and two or three persons known but not related; referees reveal capabilities that interviews and tests cannot elicit.
  • Selection decision: after all interviews the hiring manager narrows to the best fit; sometimes a runner-up is identified in case the first pick declines or does not clear testing or training.

Employment tests

Tests are instruments designed to measure selected qualities and abilities in terms of job specifications. They provide a sample of behaviour used to draw inferences about future behaviour or performance.

(i) Measures of human characteristics
GroupExamples (slide)
1. Physical characteristicsHeight, weight, senses, visual activity
2. Abilities and skillsDexterity, mathematical ability, verbal ability, intelligence, clerical skills
3. InterestsMechanical aptitudes and interests, scientific, economic, cultural interests
4. Personality traitsSociality, dominance, cooperativeness, tolerance, emotional stability
(ii) Measures of human psychology
Test typeExamples (slide)
1. AptitudeIntelligence / mental, emotional quotient, skill, aptitude, psychomotor, clerical aptitude tests
2. AchievementJob knowledge test, work sample test
3. SituationalGroup discussion, in-basket exercise
4. InterestMeasures preferences for activities
5. PersonalityObjective, projective, situation tests
6. Multi-dimensionalCombined batteries
How the exam asked it

D25 · 4A (3): “How are employment tests instrumental in the selection procedure? With suitable representations, list out the measures of human psychology and human characteristics.”

How to write it in the exam

Say first why tests matter: they are objective and uniform, predict job performance, reduce bias and filter large pools cheaply, and reveal what CVs and interviews cannot (aptitude, personality). Then draw the two diagrams above (characteristics: 4 boxes; psychology: 6 boxes) with the examples.

Interviews (slide)

StageTypes included (slide)Purpose
Preliminary interviewInformal; unstructuredQuick screen of basic qualifications and fit; saves time by rejecting clearly unsuitable candidates early.
Core interviewBackground-information, job and probing, stress, group discussion, formal and structured, panel, depth interviewIn-depth evaluation of knowledge, behaviour and suitability using structured, probing methods.
Decision-making interview(final stage)Final discussion on selection, pay and terms.
How the exam asked it

J25 · 4B (3): “Differentiate between a Preliminary Interview and a Core Interview in the recruitment process. Explain the purpose of each stage.”

How to write it in the exam

Table above, plus: preliminary is short, informal, done by HR or a junior; core is longer, planned, done by a panel or the line manager, tests depth. Mention one core type with an example (a stress interview for a customer-facing role, a panel interview for an engineering job).

4.5 Training and development: process, trends, methods

Asked in endsemN24 · Q4BD24 · Q4BM25 · Q4BN25 · Q4BD25 · Q4BM26 · Q4BJ26 · Q4B
Start here: a simple picture

A new cricketer can bat, but the team needs him to play the specific role of a death-over specialist. Teaching him exactly that, this season, is training. Preparing him to become the captain in five years through varied experiences and leadership workshops is development.

Definition

Training is acquiring specific knowledge and skills for a particular job or task; usually short-term and concerned with improving current job performance. It includes formal courses, on-the-job training or coaching sessions. Development is broader, long-term growth of the person for future roles.

The five processes of training and development (slide)

1
Needs assessmentgap between required and actual skills
→
2
Design and developmentobjectives, content, methods, materials
→
3
Deliveryconducting the training
→
4
Evaluationdid learning occur and transfer to the job?
→
5
Follow-upreinforcement, coaching, refresher

Current trends in training and development (slide)

TrendWhat it isImpact and example
1. Digital learningOnline courses, e-learning platforms, virtual classroomsAnytime, anywhere, scalable, cheaper; e.g. Google and Microsoft learning portals; Coursera for Business.
2. Personalised training programmesLearning paths tailored to each employee's role, level and gapsHigher relevance and engagement; AI recommends courses (LinkedIn Learning).
3. MicrolearningShort 3-10 minute lessons delivered in bite-sized piecesBetter retention, fits busy schedules; mobile quizzes and short videos.
4. GamificationPoints, badges, leaderboards and challenges in learningRaises motivation and completion rates; e.g. sales training with leaderboards.
5. Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) trainingProgrammes on bias, inclusion and equal opportunityInclusive culture, lower attrition, better teamwork.
6. Soft-skills developmentCommunication, teamwork, leadership, emotional intelligenceBetter collaboration and customer handling as automation takes routine tasks.

Company examples (slides): Microsoft: technical, leadership and career workshops; annual Hackathon where employees collaborate on new ideas. Google: leadership and technical training plus peer-teaching programmes where employees teach and learn from each other. Amazon: extensive on-the-job training; Career Choice pays 95% of tuition and fees for learning in high-demand fields. Starbucks: “Starbucks Experience”: online plus in-person training on customer service, coffee knowledge and drink preparation, with continuous coaching and feedback. Walmart: customer service, compliance and leadership development plus tuition assistance.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 4B: three current trends with impact and recent industry examples. D24 · 4B and M25 · 4B: discuss the process of T&D and the current trends with examples and/or representations. N25 · 4B and J26 · 4B: tech start-up founder: elaborate on 3 trends you will consider. M26 · 4B: digital marketing agency hiring freshers: any three trends.

Worked answer: tech start-up (N25 / J26) and digital marketing agency (M26)

Pick three trends and tie each to the business:

  • Microlearning: freshers learn Google Ads or React in 5-minute modules between tasks; quick, low-cost, retention-friendly; useful for a lean start-up with no spare days for classroom courses.
  • Digital / personalised learning: an LMS assigns paths (backend developer vs designer), tracks progress, scales as the team grows without trainers.
  • Gamification: certification badges and leaderboards for campaign-optimisation challenges motivate young employees and raise completion.

For each: state the trend, how you will implement it in your firm, and the impact on performance (faster ramp-up, lower attrition, higher quality). Add the T&D process as a one-line frame if the question asks for “processes”.

Training methods (slide)

On-the-job methods
  • Apprenticeship programmes: learning a skill under an experienced worker.
  • Coaching: supervisor guides and gives feedback.
  • Internship training: students or fresh graduates work in the organisation for a fixed period.
  • Job rotation: moving through different jobs to widen skills.
Off-the-job methods
  • Conferences and lectures.
  • Films / video-based learning.
  • Case study: analysing real business problems.
  • Computer modelling and simulation.
  • Vestibule training: a replica of the workplace away from the shop floor.
  • Programmed instruction: step-by-step self-paced learning materials.
How the exam asked it

D25 · 4B (3): technical organisation consulting investment and banking: list all on-the-job and off-the-job methods; illustrate one of each suited to the business, using examples and/or representation.

Worked answer

List the four on-the-job and six off-the-job methods above. On-the-job example: job rotation for a junior analyst moving through equity research, debt desk and risk teams over a year; benefits: broad exposure, cross-functional understanding. Draw a rotation cycle (Equity → Debt → Risk → Equity). Off-the-job example: case study / computer modelling: analysts model a leveraged-buyout in Excel from a real bank deal, discuss the case in groups, trainer debriefs; benefits: risk-free practice with real complexity.

Sensitivity training and manager development

Sensitivity training is a form of training whose goal is to make people more aware of their own goals and prejudices, and more sensitive to others and the dynamics of group interaction (often in unstructured group sessions, also called T-group training).

Eight considerations in ensuring the development of excellent managers (slide):

  1. Instilling a willingness to learn: managers must take advantage of new knowledge and techniques.
  2. Accelerating management development: more seminars and conferences and simple ways of transmitting new knowledge.
  3. Planning for innovation: as competition sharpens and problems become complex.
  4. Measuring and rewarding management effectively: objective performance measures, rewards, sanctions, corrective action.
  5. Tailoring information: the right information, in the right form, at the right time.
  6. Expanding research and development in tools and techniques.
  7. Developing more managerial inventories.
  8. Creating strong intellectual leadership.

4.6 Induction and orientation

Asked in endsemJ25 · Q5AN25 · Q5A
Start here: a simple picture

On the first day at a new college, a welcome talk tells you about the college, rules and culture (induction). In the first week, your department shows you your timetable, labs and teachers, and what each course expects (orientation). One introduces you to the institution; the other to your place in it.

Definition

Induction is the formal process of introducing a new employee to the organisation, its policies and culture. Orientation is a structured programme to familiarise new employees with their job roles, teams and work environment.

BasisInductionOrientation
ObjectiveWelcome the person and introduce the organisation as a wholeFamiliarise the person with the job, team and workplace
ContentHistory, vision and values, policies, rules, benefits, culture, facilities, safety, code of conductJob role and duties, reporting manager and team, tools, performance expectations, work processes
LevelOrganisation-wide, generalDepartment / job specific
TimingFirst day or first few daysFirst weeks, continues until comfortable
Conducted byHR departmentSupervisor and team
How the exam asked it

J25 · 5A (3): differentiate between orientation and induction programmes, highlighting objective and content. N25 · 5A (3): as HR manager at PhonePe, design a programme using induction (3 factors) and orientation (3 factors) and explain how it helps newcomers adapt and be engaged.

Worked answer: PhonePe programme (N25 5A)
  • Induction (organisation level): (1) vision, values and history of PhonePe; (2) company policies, data-security and compliance rules (vital for a payments firm); (3) benefits, facilities and culture, with a talk by a senior leader.
  • Orientation (job level): (1) role and duties with the job description and KPIs; (2) team introductions, buddy or mentor allocation; (3) hands-on tour of tools, systems and processes in the first weeks.

How it helps: faster cultural fit and trust, clarity of expectations, fewer early mistakes, higher engagement and lower early attrition.

4.7 The systems approach to staffing

Asked in endsemN24 · Q5AD24 · Q5AM25 · Q5AM26 · Q5AJ26 · Q5A
Start here: a simple picture

Think of a football club's squad planning. The club's strategy (play attacking football) decides how many strikers, midfielders and defenders it needs; the club checks who it already has (squad inventory); fills the gaps from the youth academy (internal) or the transfer market (external); and then keeps developing and appraising the players so the team keeps winning. Staffing a company works the same way, as one connected system, not as isolated hiring acts.

How the system flows (slide)

  1. Enterprise plans become the basis for organisation plans, which are needed to reach the enterprise objectives.
  2. The present and projected enterprise structure decides the number and kind of managers required.
  3. This demand is compared with available talent through the manager inventory (analysis of present and future needs).
  4. On the basis of that analysis, external and internal sources are used in recruitment, selection, placement, promotion and separation.
  5. Other staffing aspects: appraisal, career strategy, training and development of managers.
  6. Staffing affects leading and controlling: proper staffing facilitates both.
  7. The whole system works inside the external environment and with the internal environment (personnel policies, reward system).

The number of managers required depends on four factors (slide): size, complexity of the organisational structure, plans of the enterprise, and rate of turnover of managerial personnel.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 5A (3): how can the systems approach help HR managers of a manufacturing plant? Labelled sketch. D24 · 5A and M25 · 5A (3): describe it with a clear diagram and explain its significance in recruitment/selection. M26 · 5A (3): labelled sketch; why important for organisations? J26 · 5A (3): apply to State Bank of India to meet goals and deliver quality banking services.

Worked answers

Always draw the figure above with all boxes labelled, then apply it.

  • Manufacturing plant (N24): enterprise plan = double output next year → organisation plan = add a third shift and a new line → number and kind of supervisors/engineers required → compare with manager inventory (skills in the plant) → fill from internal (promote senior operators) or external (campus engineers) sources → recruit, select, place → appraise, plan careers, train on new machines → better leading and controlling of the line.
  • Significance (D24, M25, M26): links staffing to organisational plans; ensures right number and type of people at the right time; avoids shortages and surpluses; makes recruitment and selection systematic by using both internal and external sources; connects appraisal and training to career strategy; improves leading and controlling; adapts to the environment.
  • SBI (J26): enterprise plan = expand digital banking and rural reach; organisation plans = new digital division and branch network; number and kind of managers required (branch managers, IT, risk); manager inventory shows gaps in digital skills; internal sources (promote and transfer officers) and external sources (campus hiring, lateral IT hires through the SBI probationary-officer and specialist-officer routes); recruitment, selection, placement; appraisal and training (e.g. SBI's training institutes); resulting better leading and control yields quality service.
End of chapter

Chapter 4: summary

  • HRM manages people (planning, staffing, administration); HRD develops them (training, career, organisational development). HRM is the larger concept. Integrating both gives holistic development, strategic alignment, higher productivity and better retention.
  • Job analysis yields the job description (tasks, duties, responsibilities: the job) and the job specification (qualifications, skills, traits: the person). Know the six factors for a specification.
  • Recruitment = search and attract; 10 steps from identifying needs to onboarding. Sources: internal (promotion, transfer, demotion, retired employees, notice boards) and external (ads, institutes, agencies, walk-ins, recommendation). Challenges: talent shortage, competition, diversity, candidate experience, technology, compliance.
  • Selection: six steps (preliminary interview, application form, reference checks, tests, interview, decision). Tests measure human characteristics (physical, abilities, interests, personality) and psychology (aptitude, achievement, situational, interest, personality, multi-dimensional). Preliminary interview = quick screen; core interview = in-depth.
  • Training (short-term, job-specific) vs development (long-term). Five steps: needs assessment, design, delivery, evaluation, follow-up. Trends: digital, personalised, microlearning, gamification, DEI, soft skills. Methods: on-the-job (apprenticeship, coaching, internship, job rotation); off-the-job (conferences, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule, programmed instruction).
  • Induction introduces the organisation; orientation introduces the job, team and workplace.
  • Systems approach to staffing: plans → managers required → manager inventory → analysis → internal/external sources → recruitment...separation → appraisal, career strategy, T&D → leading and controlling, within the external and internal environment.

Most likely exam items: T&D trends and process (6 papers) · systems approach with diagram (5) · recruitment sources and steps · job description/specification · induction vs orientation · employment tests.

Chapter 5

Leadership, Motivation, Communication and Controlling

Lectures 29-36 · leaders, motivation theories, styles, committees and teams, communication, control

This is the biggest chapter and the most case-heavy. Almost every question here is a short scenario followed by “identify the style / theory / type of control and quote the lines”. The method is the same every time: name it, quote the line, explain in one sentence why. Practise that, and the marks follow.

5.1 Leadership: leaders vs managers, ingredients, qualities

Asked in endsemN24 · Q4C
Start here: a simple picture

In a ship, the captain who reads the chart, schedules the crew and checks the fuel is managing. The same captain who calms the crew in a storm and makes them believe they will reach the harbour is leading. A manager keeps the ship on the plan; a leader makes people want to sail.

Definition

Leadership is the art or process of influencing people so that they will strive willingly and enthusiastically toward the achievement of group goals. Ideally people should develop not only willingness to work but “willingness to work with zeal and confidence”: zeal is ardour, earnestness and intensity; confidence reflects experience and technical ability. Leading = influencing, guiding, commanding people.

ManagersLeaders
Focus on thingsFocus on people
Do things rightDo the right things
Plan, organise, direct, controlInspire, influence, motivate, build
Follow the rulesShape entities

Ingredients of leadership (slide)

  1. The ability to use power effectively and responsibly.
  2. The ability to understand that human beings have different motivation forces at different times and situations.
  3. The ability to inspire.
  4. The ability to act in a manner that develops a climate conducive to responding to and affecting motivations.

Qualities of an effective leader (slide)

Not arrogant; not miserly; as open as possible with subordinates; ensures troops understand what is expected; promotes competence and inspires; sees things from others' point of view; puts the organisation's needs above his own.

5.2 Motivation: motive, motivator, satisfaction, motivation; techniques

Start here: a simple picture

You are hungry (the motive); your friend promises you a biryani if you finish the assignment (the motivator); you work hard (the motivation is the drive and effort); after you eat, you feel content (satisfaction).

TermMeaning (slide)
MotiveAn inner state that energises, activates or moves and directs behaviour towards goals; the driving force behind human actions.
MotivatorThe technique used to motivate people.
SatisfactionThe contentment experienced when a want is satisfied.
MotivationThe drive and effort to satisfy a want or goal; the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals.

Motivational techniques

Positive techniques
  • Praise workers and give due credit.
  • Take sincere interest in subordinates as persons.
  • Promote healthy competition.
  • Develop pride in the workplace.
  • Delegate substantial responsibility.
  • Fair wages and individual or group incentives.
  • A suitable suggestion system.
  • Opportunities for growth and promotion.
Negative techniques
  • Reprimanding (scolding, lecturing).
  • Demotion.
  • Lay-offs.
  • Discharge.

The proper proportioning of positive and negative techniques is the mark of a skilful manager.

Special techniques (slide): money (economists and most managers place it high; behavioural scientists place it low), positive reinforcement, job enrichment (adding challenge and responsibility to the job), and participation.

5.3 Maslow's hierarchy of needs

Asked in endsemD25 · Q3CJ26 · Q3CD25 · Q5A
Start here: a simple picture

A hungry, cold person on a pavement is not thinking about career growth. Only after he gets food and a shelter does he start worrying about safety, then friends, then respect, and finally about becoming the best artist or engineer he can be. Needs are like stairs: you stand on one step before you worry about the next.

The theory says that as each need is substantially satisfied, the next need becomes dominant; a satisfied need no longer motivates. Higher-order needs are satisfied internally; lower-order needs externally.

LevelHow organisations meet it (slide 14)
PhysiologicalAdequate salary, work breaks, safe working conditions
SafetySafe working conditions, job security, fringe benefits (medical insurance, sick pay, pensions)
SocialOpportunity to interact, be accepted and have friends; parties, picnics, trips, office sports teams
EsteemMerit pay rises, recognition, challenging tasks, participation in decision making, opportunity for advancement
Self-actualisationSkill development, chance to be creative, promotions, complete control over the job

Criticism (needed for the J26 evaluation question)

  • Needs do not always follow a strict order; people may chase esteem even when safety is weak (a starving artist).
  • Different cultures and individuals rank needs differently.
  • Hard to measure whether a need is “substantially” satisfied; little empirical support for the fixed stages.
  • Ignores situational factors, e.g. the job itself, and does not explain how expectations affect effort (see Herzberg, McGregor and expectancy theory).
How the exam asked it

D25 · 3C (4): Nykaa: use Maslow's hierarchy to motivate employees at different career stages, a report on how each level influences engagement, performance and retention. J26 · 3C (4): ConnectCall five employees: identify the highest unfulfilled Maslow level for each; actions for A and D. D25 · 5A (3): X Company (infrastructure): unmet levels, how Maslow helps, critical evaluation and other models.

Worked answer: J26 3C (ConnectCall)
EmployeeEvidenceHighest unfulfilled level
A, RaviPay “just enough”; salary delayed; no night transport, “I fear walking to the bus stop”Safety (secure pay, personal safety). Physiological is barely met, but the delay threatens it too.
B, Neha“I feel invisible … colleagues don't include me … I eat lunch alone”Social / belonging
C, ArjunGood pay, house, supportive team; but “career has stopped growing”; cross-training request ignoredEsteem (advancement, challenge). If you stress self-development you may say self-actualisation; justify.
D, PriyaHigh pay, respect; wants to design a training module, “I have more to offer”Self-actualisation
E, SunilPassed over for promotion; “humiliated and underappreciated”Esteem (recognition, fair advancement)

Actions. A: pay salaries on time (fixed payroll date), provide safe night cab service and a security escort to the bus stop; this meets safety needs, a precondition for higher motivation. D: let her lead the design of the new onboarding module, give creative control and sponsor leadership training; this lets her use her potential (self-actualisation).

Worked answers: D25 3C (Nykaa) and D25 5A (X Company)

Nykaa, by career stage: new joiner → physiological and safety (fair pay, safe stores, job security, benefits) → retention; early career → social (team culture, mentors) → engagement; mid-career → esteem (recognition, promotion, titles) → performance; senior → self-actualisation (creative projects, leadership of new initiatives) → commitment. For each level state: need, how Nykaa meets it, effect on engagement, performance, retention.

X Company: poor working conditions → physiological/safety; non-competitive pay → physiological/safety (and esteem); limited career growth → esteem and self-actualisation; weak culture → social. Application: improve conditions and pay first, build team culture, create promotion paths, then empowerment. Critical evaluation: sequence not rigid, culture-dependent, hard to measure, no explanation of dissatisfaction vs satisfaction; complement with Herzberg (hygiene fixes the first four problems, motivators fix growth), McGregor (Theory Y style), and expectancy theory (effort depends on perceived reward).

5.4 Herzberg's two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory

Asked in endsemD24 · Q3CM25 · Q3CN25 · Q3CM26 · Q3C
Start here: a simple picture

A mobile phone needs a charged battery (hygiene) to work at all, but a flawless battery does not make you love the phone. What makes you love it is the camera and features (motivators). Similarly, a decent salary stops an employee from being unhappy but does not make him passionate; interesting work and recognition do.

Definition

Herzberg's two-factor theory (also motivation-hygiene or dual-factor theory) argues that there are separate sets of mutually exclusive factors in the workplace that cause job satisfaction or dissatisfaction. The opposite of satisfaction is no satisfaction, not dissatisfaction.

Satisfiers: motivators (intrinsic)Dissatisfiers: hygiene factors (extrinsic)
Performance and achievement
Recognition
Job status
Responsibility
Opportunities for advancement
Personal growth
The work itself		Salary
Working conditions
The physical workspace
Relationship with colleagues
Relationship with supervisor
Quality of supervisor
Policies and rules
Improving these increases job satisfaction.Improving these decreases job dissatisfaction, but does not motivate.

The four combinations (slide)

Low motivatorsHigh motivators
High hygieneEmployees have few complaints but are not motivatedIdeal: no complaints and motivated
Low hygieneWorst: not motivated and have complaintsMotivated to work but have complaints

Maslow vs Herzberg (slide 18)

Herzberg's motivators (achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement) map to Maslow's self-actualisation and esteem. Herzberg's hygiene factors (interpersonal relations, company policy and administration, salary, supervision, working conditions) map to Maslow's belonging, safety and physiological needs.

How the exam asked it

D24 · 3C (4): Innovatech: advise the CEO which theory to apply to two teams. M25 · 3C (4): corporate strategies that fulfil each Herzberg factor and their impact on retention and performance. N25 · 3C (4): Lenskart: four factors each. M26 · 3C (4): Sameer's exit interview.

Worked answers

M26 Sameer: Hygiene factors (satisfied): “My salary is good and the office is comfortable” (salary, working conditions) → no dissatisfaction from these. Motivators (missing): “I never receive any appreciation” (recognition); “doing the same tasks for three years” (the work itself, personal growth); “no growth” (advancement); “never gives me any challenging responsibilities” (responsibility). So Sameer is not dissatisfied by hygiene but is demotivated because motivators are absent; the company should offer recognition, job enrichment and promotion paths. Add 3-4 lines explaining the theory.

N25 Lenskart (four each): Hygiene: salary and incentives; store working conditions and shifts; supervision quality of store managers; company policies (leave, targets). Motivators: recognition (employee of the month); achievement (sales and customer-satisfaction milestones); advancement (path from optometrist to store manager); responsibility and growth (training, leading a store project). Employees with similar conditions differ because hygiene is equal but motivators vary store to store.

M25 corporate approach: Hygiene: competitive pay (Infosys, TCS), safe and comfortable offices (Google campuses), fair policies, good supervision. Motivators: recognition programmes, stretch assignments, job enrichment, promotions and learning budgets (Amazon Career Choice). Impact: hygiene reduces attrition; motivators raise performance and engagement.

D24 Innovatech: Team 1 (Innovation): already works well with flexibility; frustrated by unclear goals and no growth, so apply motivators (clear challenging goals, growth paths, recognition), which is also Theory Y and Maslow's esteem and self-actualisation. Team 2 (Support): structured, repetitive, dissatisfied with routine; first fix hygiene (fair pay, shift comfort, supervision) then add job rotation and enrichment, performance incentives and recognition; clear structure fits Theory X-style direction for routine tasks. Principal theory: Herzberg's two-factor (it explains both teams); mention McGregor as supporting.

5.5 McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y

Asked in endsemN24 · Q3CD24 · Q3CJ25 · Q3C
Start here: a simple picture

Two class monitors. Monitor X believes classmates are lazy, so he watches everyone, threatens to report them and still thinks nobody will work. Monitor Y believes they are capable, gives them responsibility and trust, and usually gets them to do well. Their beliefs about people decide their style.

Theory X gives importance to supervision; Theory Y stresses rewards and recognition.

Theory X (traditional belief)
  • The average employee dislikes work and tries to escape it.
  • Must be persuaded, compelled or warned with punishment; close supervision; dictatorial style.
  • Ranks job security on top; little ambition.
  • Dislikes responsibility; resists change.
  • Needs formal direction.
Theory Y (belief based on research)
  • Work can be as natural as rest or play.
  • People use self-direction and self-control if committed.
  • Rewarding jobs bring loyalty and commitment.
  • The average person can learn to accept and seek responsibility.
  • Creativity, resourcefulness and innovation are widely spread and can be used.
BasisTheory XTheory Y
MeaningHigh supervision and control; centralisationWorkers self-directed and self-motivated; active in decisions
WorkDislikes workWork is natural
AmbitionLittle to noneHighly ambitious
ResponsibilityAvoidsAccepts and seeks
Leadership styleAutocraticDemocratic
Direction / controlConstant direction; tight controlLittle direction; lenient control
AuthorityCentralisedDecentralised
Self-motivationAbsentPresent
Focus on (Maslow)Physiological and security needsSocial, esteem and self-actualisation needs
How the exam asked it

N24 · 3C (4): Analyse Theory X and Y, how a manager develops strategies to motivate employees; corporate examples. J25 · 3C (4): corporate strategies that fulfil each factor of Theory X and Y; impact on retention and performance.

Worked answer (corporate strategies and impact)
  • Theory X strategies: tight targets and call monitoring in BPOs and call centres; assembly-line time standards (Maruti, Toyota lines); strict attendance and compliance systems in banks. Impact: good for routine, safety-critical or inexperienced settings; short-term control and output; but risks resentment, low creativity, attrition.
  • Theory Y strategies: Google's autonomy and 20%-time style projects; Infosys and TCS empowered project teams; flexible work, participative goal setting (MBO), job enrichment, recognition. Impact: higher engagement, innovation and retention; but needs capable, mature employees and can drift without direction.
  • Conclusion: use X for new or routine work, Y for skilled, creative work; the best managers blend them according to the situation.

5.6 Leadership styles based on the use of authority (Lewin)

Asked in endsemN24 · Q4CN25 · Q4CD25 · Q4C
Start here: a simple picture

Three captains in a school cricket team. Captain A sets the batting order and bowling changes himself and never asks (autocratic). Captain B asks players for views on field placement, then decides (democratic). Captain C says “you are all senior, sort it out” (free rein).

Definition

Leadership style is the manner and approach of providing direction, implementing plans and motivating people. Kurt Lewin (1939) and his researchers established three major styles.

StyleFeatures (slide)Use whenExamples / drawbacks
Autocratic
(power with the leader)		Commands and expects compliance; tells employees what and how, without advice; all decision power with the leader; leads by ability to withhold or give rewards and punishmentLeader has all the information, time is short, employees are well motivated; rare, emergencyMilitary, manufacturing, construction. Drawback: low initiative, resentment
Democratic / participative
(power shared)		Consults subordinates and encourages participation; leader keeps the final decision; sign of strength, not weaknessLeader has part of the information and employees the rest; mutual benefitBetter decisions, team ownership. Drawback: slower
Delegative / free rein
(power with employees)		Leader uses power very little; employees set their own goals and means; leader still responsibleEmployees can analyse the situation and know what to do (experts)Research teams, senior specialists. Drawback: lack of direction

Forces that influence the style (slide): time available; relationships based on respect and trust; who has the information; how well employees are trained and how well you know the task; internal conflicts; stress levels; type of task (structured or complicated); laws or established procedures.

Leadership as a continuum (Tannenbaum and Schmidt)

Instead of choosing between authoritarian and democratic, the theory offers a range of styles depending on the freedom the leader grants. The right style depends on the leader, followers and situation.

How the exam asked it

N24 · 4C (4): TechNova: the most suitable leadership style for the Product Development and Technical Support departments, with reasons. N25 · 4C (4): TCS scenarios: identify the styles based on the use of authority, quoting lines. D25 · 4C (4): analyse authority leadership styles and evaluate their impact on motivation and productivity.

Worked answers

N25 TCS:

  • “the same manager conducts brainstorming sessions, encourages team members to share ideas, and collectively decides on the technology stack and workflow” → Democratic / participative (planning phase: leader consults and shares power).
  • “experienced developers are given autonomy to choose coding practices and manage their schedules, with minimal supervision” → Free rein.
  • “the project manager takes full control, assigns tasks without discussion, and enforces strict timelines” → Autocratic (critical deadline needs quick decisions).
  • “senior QA engineers are given full freedom to choose tools, create test cases, and schedule their work, with minimal managerial intervention” → Free rein again.

N24 TechNova: Product Development (creative engineers who feel stifled by oversight, flourish on brainstorming) → democratic / participative (leaning to free rein for senior designers). Technical Support (fast-paced, scripts and procedures, uniform protocol) → autocratic / directive (structured tasks need clear rules and quick decisions); a warm, supportive touch prevents burnout.

D25 impact: autocratic: fast decisions and discipline but lower motivation, creativity and higher attrition; democratic: high motivation and commitment but slower; free rein: high motivation for experts but risk of confusion. Productivity is highest when style matches the task and the people.

5.7 Likert's four systems of managing

Asked in endsemD24 · Q4CM25 · Q4CJ26 · Q4C
Start here: a simple picture

Four head chefs in four kitchens. In Kitchen 1 the chef shouts and threatens; in Kitchen 2 he gives small rewards but still decides everything; in Kitchen 3 he listens to cooks' ideas on the menu but keeps final say; in Kitchen 4 the whole kitchen decides the menu together. Likert called these four systems, from harsh to fully participative.

Rensis Likert and his associates at the University of Michigan studied managers over three decades across 200 organisations and proposed four systems of management (also viewed as leadership styles).

SystemTrust and confidenceMotivationCommunicationDecisions and responsibilityTeamwork
1. Exploitative authoritativeNo trust or confidence in subordinatesFear and punishment, occasional rewardsDownward onlyDecisions at the top, imposed; subordinates not free to discussVery little
2. Benevolent authoritativePatronising confidence and trustRewards and some fear and punishmentSome upward; asks some ideasSome delegation with close control; responsibility at managerial levelsVery little
3. ConsultativeSubstantial but not completeRewards, occasional punishment, some participationUp and downBroad policy at top, specific decisions at lower levels; responsibility widely spreadFair amount
4. ParticipativeComplete trust and confidenceRewards and involvement in the jobDown, up and sidewaysDecision making throughout the organisation; goals widespreadHigh level

Likert found that managers using System 4 had the greatest success: departments and companies were more effective in setting and achieving goals and generally more productive.

How the exam asked it

D24 · 4C and M25 · 4C (4): “Explain, with a neat sketch, Likert's Four Systems of Managing and examine the effect of each system on employee motivation and productivity.” J26 · 4C (4): Reliance Retail Expansion: identify Likert's systems by quoting lines.

Worked answers

D24 / M25 effects: System 1 → fear, low motivation, high attrition; short-run output only. System 2 → compliance for rewards, limited motivation; productivity moderate. System 3 → good motivation through involvement; high productivity. System 4 → highest motivation, commitment and productivity; but needs trust, skilled people and time.

J26 Reliance:

  • “Reliance forms cross-functional teams to co-create solutions … decision-making is collaborative, and employees feel empowered to innovate” → System 4, participative.
  • “senior leaders start offering incentives and recognition … While decisions remain centralized, managers are allowed minor flexibility” → System 2, benevolent authoritative (rewards plus close control).
  • “top management imposes strict targets and policies without consulting store managers … Decisions are centralized … pressure to meet deadlines” → System 1, exploitative authoritative.
  • “management actively seeks input from regional managers and tech teams. Suggestions are considered before final decisions” → System 3, consultative (consults but keeps the final decision).

5.8 The Managerial Grid (Blake and Mouton)

Asked in endsemJ25 · Q4CM26 · Q4C
Start here: a simple picture

Two questions about any boss: How much does he care about getting the work done? and How much does he care about his people? Plot the answers on a 9 x 9 grid and you have the managerial grid.

A self-assessment tool by Robert R. Blake and Jane S. Mouton (1960s). Concern for production runs along the horizontal axis (1 low, 9 high), concern for people along the vertical axis; 81 positions, five key styles.

StyleConcern: people / productionDescription (slide)Pros and cons
1,1 ImpoverishedLow / lowMinimum effort to get required work done and sustain membership; managers have abandoned the job and act only as messengers.Pro: none. Con: disorganisation, ineffective.
1,9 Country ClubHigh / lowThoughtful attention to people; friendly, relaxed atmosphere; no coordinated effort for objectives.Pro: happy, motivated people. Con: low output, poor results.
9,1 Task / Authority-complianceLow / highEfficiency by arranging work so that human elements interfere minimally; dictatorial; based on Theory X.Pro: high output short-term. Con: high turnover, low creativity.
5,5 Middle of the roadMedium / mediumBalance of work and morale; adequate performance; goals not set too high.Pro: stability. Con: only average performance.
9,9 Team managementHigh / highWork from committed people; common stake; trust and respect; based on Theory Y; most effective.Pro: high output, satisfaction, innovation. Con: takes time and skilled people.
How the exam asked it

J25 · 4C (4): PSN Corporation: identify and explain the 4 leadership styles quoting lines; pros and cons of each. M26 · 4C (4): Metro Logistics: identify the styles of AK, BK, CK, DK using the grid; draw and label the grid (2 + 2 marks).

Worked answers

M26 Metro Logistics: AK = 9,1 Task management (“extremely focused on delivery targets … rarely asks about personal problems”; best on-time record but high complaints). BK = 1,9 Country Club (“popular … organises team lunches … avoids conflicts”; happy staff but misses deadlines). CK = 5,5 Middle of the road (“balanced approach … meets most deadlines, turnover low”: moderate on both). DK = 9,9 Team management (“high targets” + “weekly one-on-one meetings … recognition … team-building”; highest on-time delivery and lowest turnover). Then draw the grid above and mark all five (include 1,1 Impoverished in the figure).

J25 PSN: (1) “prioritize employee well-being over productivity … relaxed and friendly work environment” → Country Club (1,9): pros happy staff; con productivity decline. (2) “managers adopted a hands-off approach, avoiding difficult decisions and failing to set clear expectations … employees lacked direction, motivation, and accountability” → Impoverished (1,1): no real pros; performance stagnates. (3) “new managers were very target-oriented … focused solely on developing efficient operations … little concern for employee well-being” → Task management (9,1): better production returns but choked creativity, teamwork, high attrition. (4) “unwavering dedication to both people and production, fostering a collaborative work environment” → Team management (9,9): high-performance teams, innovation, career development; con: requires investment in time and training.

5.9 Committees, groups, teams and group development

Asked in endsemD24 · Q5BM25 · Q5BM26 · Q5B
Start here: a simple picture

Planning a college fest: the committee is the formal body given the job (“the sponsorship committee”); a group is anyone who works together interdependently (the volunteers at the gate); a team is a small group with complementary skills, one shared goal and mutual accountability (the 6-member stage crew who all sink or swim together).

CommitteeGroupTeam
Definition (slide)A group of persons to whom, as a group, some matter is committed (board, commission, task force)Two or more people acting interdependently in a unified manner toward common goalsA small number of people with complementary skills committed to a common purpose, performance goals and approach for which they hold themselves mutually accountable
NatureFormal or informal, permanent or temporary; some only recommend, some decideShare goals, interact, have roles, are part of a larger group, develop normsSelf-managing, cross-functional, problem-solving (quality circles), virtual
AccountabilityCollective; can split responsibilityIndividual membersMutual and joint
SkillsRepresentatives of interestsMixedComplementary skills by design

Four stages of group development (slide)

1
Formingmembers get to know each other
→
2
Stormingmembers determine the objective and conflict arises
→
3
Normingthe group agrees on norms and rules of behaviour
→
4
Performingthe group gets down to the task
Example

Example (a college project team of five): Forming: first meeting, polite introductions, unclear roles. Storming: disagreement over the topic and who leads. Norming: they agree on weekly meetings, a leader and task split. Performing: they build and test the prototype smoothly and meet the deadline.

Reasons for using committees
  • Group deliberation and judgment ("two heads are better than one").
  • Dominant logic / shared worldview of top decision makers.
  • Fear of too much authority in a single person.
  • Representation of interested groups.
  • Coordination of departments, plans and policies.
  • Transmission and sharing of information.
  • Consolidation of splintered authority.
  • Motivation through participation.
Disadvantages and misuse
  • Costly (time of many people).
  • Compromise at the least common denominator.
  • Indecision; split responsibility.
  • A few persons may dominate the majority.
  • Should not replace a manager, be used for research, for unimportant decisions or for decisions beyond the participants' authority.

Team building (slide): team members must believe the purpose is worthwhile, meaningful and urgent; select members for needed skills (technical, problem-solving, human relations); set rules (attendance, confidentiality, fact-based discussion, everyone contributing); identify goals and tasks early; encourage with recognition, feedback and rewards. Types: self-managing team (various skills to carry out a relatively complete task); virtual team (members in different locations, may not report to the manager or even work for the same organisation).

How the exam asked it

D24 · 5B and M25 · 5B (3): summarise the stages of group development; what distinguishes a committee, group and team? M26 · 5B (3): explain the four stages with a brief explanation of each and relevant examples.

How to write it in the exam

Four stages (each with 1-2 lines and an example, as above), then the comparison table. A clean flow of four boxes earns the diagram marks.

5.10 Communication: process, types and barriers

Asked in endsemJ25 · Q5BN25 · Q5BN24 · Q5BJ26 · Q5BM26 · Q5C
Start here: a simple picture

Passing a message in a game of “Chinese whispers”: what the first person says is not what the last person hears. Every step (thinking, wording, speaking, hearing, interpreting) can distort the message, and the only way to check is for the listener to say it back (feedback). Business communication is the same game, with money at stake.

Definition

Communication is the means by which people are linked together in an organisation to achieve common goals. Group activity is impossible without it because coordination and change cannot be effected. It is essential for internal functioning (it integrates planning, organising, staffing, leading and controlling) and for relating the enterprise to its external environment (customers, suppliers, stockholders, government, community).

The communication process (slide)

  1. Sender has a thought or idea and encodes it in a form understood by both.
  2. The message is transmitted through a channel (oral, written, memo, computer, telephone, TV).
  3. The receiver receives and decodes it; decoding depends on knowledge of the subject, experience, trust and relationship with the sender. Effective communication occurs only if the receiver understands exactly as intended.
  4. Feedback confirms the receiver got and interpreted it correctly (verbal or non-verbal).
  5. Noise can derail the process: physical (static, traffic), physiological (hunger, fatigue), technical (slow connection, faulty mic), organisational (unclear channels), cultural, psychological (distracting thoughts, biases), semantic (wrong words, jargon).

Nine types of communication (slide)

#TypeKey points
1FormalOfficially created procedure for flow between positions: memos, intranet, meetings, conferences, letters, notice boards, emails from managers.
2InformalOutside the recognised system: conversations and the grapevine. Networks: single strand, cluster, probability chain.
3DownwardFrom higher to lower levels (instructions, policies, memos); time-consuming and information is often lost or distorted.
4UpwardFrom subordinates to superiors; often filtered, especially bad news; needs an environment where subordinates feel free.
5Crosswise / horizontalBetween people at the same level, different responsibility areas (e.g. HR and Marketing heads).
6DiagonalAmong people at different levels with no direct reporting relation; speeds up coordination (e.g. floor manager with Sales team).
7WrittenRecords, reference, legal defence, uniformity; but paperwork, poor expression, no immediate feedback.
8OralFace to face or presentation; speedy interchange with immediate feedback.
9Non-verbalFacial expressions and gestures; may reinforce or contradict the words.
How the exam asked it

J25 · 5B (3): corporate communication with block diagrams and its process. N25 · 5B (3): apply the communication process to explain how information flows in an organisation, with a block diagram. N24 · 5B (3): three common barriers in a technology organisation and ways to address them. J26 · 5B (3): ICICI Bank: three barriers and practical strategies.

Worked answers

Corporate communication (J25): draw the figure from slide 76: the internal environment (planning, organising, staffing, leading, controlling) linked both ways to communication, which in turn links both ways to the external environment (customers, suppliers, stockholders, government, community, others); then draw and explain the process loop above.

Information flow (N25): use the flow figure and the process: the MD (sender) encodes a new policy, passes it through the heads (downward), who pass it on; staff give feedback upward; heads coordinate horizontally; the floor manager clarifies diagonally with Sales. Note which medium (email, meeting) suits each.

Barriers to effective communication and how to overcome them

Barrier (slide)ExampleRemedy
Lack of planningAn unplanned announcement confuses staffPlan the message, purpose and channel
Un-clarified assumptionsManager assumes team knows the deadlineState assumptions; confirm understanding
Semantic distortion“We sell for less” (less than what?)Use clear, simple, familiar words
Poorly expressed messages; loss by transmissionMessage distorted along a chain of levelsShort, direct channels; written confirmation
Poor retention; poor listening and premature evaluationEngineer misses a key spec in a meetingActive listening; minutes and summaries
Distrust, threat and fearStaff hide bad newsOpen, trust-building culture
Insufficient time to adjust to changeNew software announced a day before useEarly notice, training
Information overload100 emails a dayPrioritise, filter, dashboards
Selective perception; attitudes; status and power differences; too many levelsJuniors do not question seniorsOpen-door policy, flatter structure, feedback channels

Towards effective communication (slide)

  • Clarify the idea before sending; encode and decode with symbols familiar to both.
  • Plan, considering the needs of the receivers; mind tone of voice and language congruence.
  • Communication is complete only when the message is understood; it also deals with emotions.
  • Effective communication is the responsibility of both sender and receiver.

Ten listening guidelines (slide): stop talking; put the talker at ease; show you want to listen; remove distraction; empathise; be patient; hold your temper; go easy with arguments and criticism; ask questions. Written communication: simple words, short familiar words, personal pronouns, examples, short sentences and paragraphs, active verbs, no unnecessary words.

Worked answers: N24 5B (technology organisation) and J26 5B (ICICI Bank)
  • Technology organisation: (1) Semantic / jargon: engineers and business teams use different technical terms → use plain language and a shared glossary. (2) Information overload: too many Slack and email threads → set channel rules, summaries, priority tags. (3) Status and power differences / fear: juniors hide bugs → open feedback culture, blameless reviews.
  • ICICI Bank: (1) Too many levels / loss in transmission: policy changes reach branches late and distorted → direct digital circulars with confirmation. (2) Poor listening and un-clarified assumptions: staff misinterpret customer-service rules → briefings, FAQs, read-back. (3) Distrust and fear: employees avoid reporting errors → grievance channels and non-punitive reporting.

5.11 Controlling: the process, standards, types, techniques

Asked in endsemD24 · Q5CM25 · Q5CN24 · Q5CJ25 · Q5CN25 · Q5CD25 · Q5CM26 · Q5CJ26 · Q5C
Start here: a simple picture

A student plans to study 3 hours daily (plan). Every night she notes how much she actually studied (measure), compares with 3 hours (compare), sees she is 40 minutes short (deviation), finds the cause is phone use (analyse), decides to switch the phone to silent (corrective plan) and does it (implement). Controlling is the same loop for a business.

Definition

Controlling is verifying whether everything occurs in conformity with the plan adopted, the instructions issued and principles established; its object is to point out weaknesses and errors in order to rectify them and prevent recurrence (Fayol). It applies to things, people and actions. In Koontz's words it is the measurement and correction of performance to make sure enterprise objectives and plans are accomplished. Planning and controlling are closely linked: plans are the yardsticks, so controls require plans. Control is the function of every manager.

The eight steps in controlling (slide 98)

1
Establishment of standardsyardsticks from the plan
→
2
Actual performancewhat is really happening
→
3
Measure actual performancequantity, quality, time, cost
→
4
Compare actual with standard
→
5
Identification of deviationspositive or negative
→
6
Analysis of causes of deviations
→
7
Program of corrective actions
→
8
Implementation of corrections
Example

Example: a bakery with a plan to bake 500 loaves a day with fewer than 20 burnt. (1) Standard: 500 loaves, under 20 burnt. (2-3) Actual performance measured at day end: 440 loaves, 45 burnt. (4) Compare. (5) Deviation: 60 loaves short, 25 extra burnt. (6) Cause: oven thermostat faulty and a new baker. (7) Plan: repair oven, train baker. (8) Implement and check next week.

Establishing standards (slide)

Standards are simply criteria of performance: selected points in the entire planning program at which measures of performance are made so that managers receive signals about how things are going and do not have to watch every step. A standard is a unit of measurement that serves as a reference point for evaluating results; goals, objectives, quotas and targets also serve as standards. Examples: sales quotas, budgets, job deadlines, market share, profit margins. Such points are often called critical points (key result areas), because controlling every detail is impossible.

Type of standardWhat it isExamples
PhysicalQuantities of products or services, number of customers, quality of product or serviceUnits produced, calls handled
TechnicalMachine tolerances, acceptable quality levels, items per hour, specificationsDefect rate under 1%, items per hour on a line
MonetaryExpressed in rupeesLabour cost, selling cost, material cost, sales revenue, gross profit
ManagerialReports, regulations, performance evaluation; focused on key areasAppraisal ratings, compliance reports
TimeSpeed and deadlinesDelivery within 48 hours; launch by March

Three types of control (slide)

TypeDefinition (slide)Example
Feed-forward (pre-action, preventive)Allows managers to anticipate problems before they ariseChecking raw-material quality, forecasting demand, hiring and training before launch, buffer stock
Concurrent (real-time)Gives managers immediate feedback on how efficiently inputs are being transformed into outputsSupervisor watching the line, real-time defect monitoring, live dashboards
Feedback (post-action)Gives information about results, e.g. customers' reactions to goods and servicesCustomer surveys, annual audits, results review
How the exam asked it

N24 · 5C (4): TechGear: two types of control by quoting lines; two critical point standards by quoting lines. J25 · 5C (4): SmartGadgets: types of control with lines and significance. M26 · 5C (4): Professor Mehta: three types with lines and significance. J26 · 5C (4): three types of control in Reliance Jio. N25 · 5C (4): four types of standards at Micromax. D24, M25, D25 · 5C (4): eight steps with block diagram and a common example.

Worked answers

N24 TechGear

  • Feed-forward: “The supply chain manager proactively orders additional components and materials”; “The human resources team hires 25 temporary workers and schedules 3 hours of overtime”; “marketing team … conducts extensive market research. They project that the demand will exceed … planned production capacity” → actions before the problem (shortage) arises.
  • Feedback: “850 customers provided feedback through surveys and online reviews … issues with battery life and software glitches”; “The product development team analyzed customer feedback and identified that a software update is needed”; “enhance battery optimization in the next production run” → corrections after results.
  • Critical point standards: (1) “planned production capacity (2000 units)” = physical standard to compare orders against; (2) “goal of 100% customer satisfaction” = quality / managerial standard against which the 850 reviews are measured; (also “next production run starting in the 1st week of March” = time standard).

J25 SmartGadgets: Feed-forward: “negotiates long-term contracts with multiple-chip suppliers across different regions, reducing dependence on a single source”; “increase the semiconductor inventory by 75%, ensuring buffer stock” → prevents a shortage. Concurrent: “real-time monitoring detects … higher-than-usual number of defective earbuds. The production manager immediately halts the faulty line, identifies a calibration issue … and rectifies the problem before its escalation” → correction during production. Significance: feed-forward prevents disruption; concurrent limits waste and keeps quality, together protecting supply and customers.

M26 Professor Mehta: Concurrent: “asks the students sitting at the last bench, ‘Can you hear me clearly?’” and monthly committee meetings where “the professor reviews these feedback points and makes adjustments immediately” → correction while teaching. Feedback: “after 36 classes, you can tell me my faults. I can only improve next semester” → results after the course. Feed-forward: “institute sometimes swaps the timetable … Thursday follows Friday's schedule … ensures all subjects get their required number of classes” → anticipates holiday losses. Significance: concurrent fixes problems at once; feedback improves the next cycle; feed-forward prevents the problem.

J26 Reliance Jio: Feed-forward: network capacity planning and tower maintenance before festival peaks, vetting of device and vendor quality, training of customer-care staff → anticipates problems. Concurrent: real-time network-monitoring dashboards, live call-quality alarms, supervisors listening to live support calls → fix as it happens. Feedback: NPS and customer surveys, complaint analysis, monthly churn and revenue review → learn and improve outcomes. Show how each helps managers anticipate, monitor and evaluate.

N25 Micromax (any four standards): Physical: units of phones produced and shipped per month → decide production scheduling. Technical: battery life, defect rate under a set level, screen tolerance → protects quality and reduces returns. Monetary: cost per handset, gross margin, selling cost → pricing decisions to keep phones affordable. Time: days from order to delivery, launch dates → supply planning and competitiveness. (Managerial: appraisal and compliance reports.) For each, state the impact on decisions and outcomes.

D24, M25, D25 (8 steps): draw the eight-box flow above and run one example through every step (the bakery or a delivery firm; for instance a courier standard of 95% on-time deliveries, actual 88%, cause: shortage of riders, corrective plan: recruit 20 riders).

Direct control and preventive control (slide)

Direct controlPreventive control
Trace the cause of an unsatisfactory result back to the responsible persons and get them to correct their practices.Develop better managers who skilfully apply principles, concepts and techniques and a systems view, thereby eliminating results caused by poor management.
Based on negative deviations of performance from plan.Principle: “the higher the quality of managers and their subordinates, the less the need for direct control”.
Assumptions: person will take corrective action at the right time; performance can be measured; personal responsibility exists; time spent is warranted; mistakes are discovered in time.Assumptions: qualified, experienced managers make minimum errors; management fundamentals can be used to measure performance; their application can be evaluated.
Causes of negative deviation (7): uncertainty, lack of knowledge, experience or judgment, and failure of the above assumptions.Advantages: psychological (managers know what is expected), higher accuracy in assigning responsibility, encourages self-control, lightens the managerial burden.

Management control techniques (self-study material, included for the exam)

Three categories: budgetary controls, non-budgetary controls and network techniques, plus overall control devices.

1. Budgetary control

A budget is a single-use plan that details the resources (usually financial) required for a program, project or activity. Budgetary control compares actual results with the budgeted, to approve accomplishments or to remedy differences.

GroupTypesMeaning
Financial budgetCash budget; capital expenditure budget; balance-sheet budgetSources and uses of cash; cost of major assets; forecast of assets and liabilities
Operating budgetSales/revenue; expense; profit budgetPlanned operations in financial terms
Non-monetary budgetLabour (hours), space, production (units)Expressed in non-financial terms

Variable (flexible) budget varies with sales volume or output, avoiding rigidity. Zero-base budgeting divides programs into “packages” of goals, activities and resources and costs each from base zero every period, rather than only looking at changes from last period.

Dangers in budgeting: over-budgeting of minor expenses (deprives managers of freedom); budget goals overriding enterprise objectives; hiding inefficiency; causing inflexibility.

2. Non-budgetary control devices
  • Statistical data (trends, charts, averages; compared to a standard).
  • Special reports and analysis for problem areas.
  • Operational audit: regular independent appraisal by internal auditors of accounting, financial and other operations; in its best form, weighing actual results against plans.
  • Personal observation (“managing by walking around”).
3. Time-event network analysis
  • CPM (Critical Path Method): deterministic; uses a single time estimate per activity.
  • PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique): probabilistic; uses three estimates: optimistic (o), most likely (m), pessimistic (p).

Expected time te = (o + 4m + p) / 6, variance σ² = ((p − o) / 6)²

Example

An activity with o = 2, m = 5, p = 14 days: te = (2 + 4 × 5 + 14)/6 = 36/6 = 6 days. Variance = ((14 − 2)/6)² = 2² = 4, so σ = 2 days. The pessimistic tail pulls the expected time above the most likely 5 days.

  • Gantt chart: shows activities (bars) against time; the position and length of each bar show start, duration and end, so you can see overlaps, progress and dependencies at a glance.
4. Overall control devices

Needed because ordinary controls cover parts of the enterprise, and because decentralised divisions need an overall check. Generally financial in nature.

  • Budget summaries and reports: a resume of all individual budgets showing sales volume, costs, profits, capital use and ROI in proper relation; guide for corrective action.
  • Profit and loss control: each division or department calculates its revenue and expenses; profit is the standard. Works best in product and territorial divisions. Limitations: high accounting cost, departments competing, duplication of records, may be inadequate alone.
  • Return on investment (ROI): ratio of earnings to capital employed; ROI = (earnings / sales) × (sales / total investment) = profit margin × capital turnover. Advantages: locates weaknesses (e.g. rising inventories lower ROI), focuses on the central objective, works well with decentralisation, compares units and firms. Limitations: information availability, over-emphasis on financial ratios, rigidity in new investment, no benchmark of a “reasonable” return.
End of chapter

Chapter 5: summary

  • Leadership is influencing people to strive willingly with zeal and confidence. Managers do things right (plan, organise, control); leaders do the right things (inspire, influence). Motive, motivator, satisfaction and motivation are four different ideas.
  • Maslow: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation; the next need dominates once the previous is substantially satisfied. Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. McGregor: Theory X (controls, autocratic) vs Theory Y (trust, democratic).
  • Styles: by authority: autocratic, democratic, free rein. Likert: exploitative authoritative, benevolent authoritative, consultative, participative (System 4 best). Managerial grid: 1,1; 1,9; 9,1; 5,5; 9,9 (team management is best). Tannenbaum-Schmidt: a continuum depending on leader, followers and situation.
  • Committee (formal body charged with a matter), group (interdependent people), team (complementary skills, mutual accountability). Group stages: forming, storming, norming, performing.
  • Communication process: sender, encoding, transmission, reception, decoding, receiver, feedback, plus noise. Nine types; barriers include semantic distortion, overload, poor listening, fear and too many levels. Remedy: clarity, feedback, listening, shorter channels.
  • Controlling: 8 steps (standards → actual performance → measure → compare → deviations → causes → corrective program → implementation). Standards: physical, technical, monetary, managerial, time. Types: feed-forward (before), concurrent (during), feedback (after).
  • Techniques: budgetary (fixed/flexible/zero-base), non-budgetary (statistics, reports, audit, observation), network (PERT with te = (o + 4m + p)/6, CPM, Gantt), overall (budget summaries, P&L, ROI). Direct control corrects the person; preventive control develops better managers.

Most likely exam items: case → identify style / theory / type of control with quoted lines · Herzberg and Maslow application · eight steps of control with a diagram · communication barriers and process · group stages.

Last-night cheat sheet: every list you must know

Read this the night before. If any line feels unfamiliar, go back to its chapter (the headings below match the sections).

Chapter 1: Basis of management
  • Functions: planning, organising, staffing, leading, controlling.
  • Fayol: 14 principles (division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction ... esprit de corps).
  • Mintzberg: 10 roles: interpersonal (figurehead, leader, liaison), informational (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson), decisional (entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator).
  • Systems approach: inputs → transformation → outputs, with feedback, in an open system.
  • CSR, ethics, trust, international management: see section summaries.
Chapter 2: Planning
  • Types of plans (8): mission, objectives, strategy, policy, procedure, rule, programme, budget.
  • Steps (8): opportunities, objectives, premises, alternatives, compare, choose, supporting plans, budgets.
  • MBO: Drucker 1954; joint objective setting, periodic review, reward.
  • Strategy tools (5): critical question analysis, SWOT/TOWS, Blue Ocean, BCG, Porter.
  • TOWS: SO, ST, WO, WT. BCG: star, cash cow, question mark, dog. Porter: cost leadership, differentiation, focus.
  • Blue Ocean ERRC: eliminate, reduce, raise, create.
Chapter 3: Organising
  • 4 steps: identify activities, group activities, classify authority, build authority-responsibility relationships.
  • 8 factors of span: training, delegation, planning, rate of change, communication, kind of activity, kind of organisation, level.
  • Urwick (10): unity of objectives, org efficiency, specialisation, span, scalar chain, unity of command, delegation, parity, flexibility, functional definition.
  • Departmentation (8): numbers, time, function, territory, product, process, customer, matrix.
  • Line: simplest, top-down, unified control, no specialists. Line and staff: compromise, specialisation, specialists attached, command stays with line.
  • Delegation (4): results expected, assign tasks, delegate authority, create obligation.
Chapter 4: Talent acquisition
  • Recruitment (10 steps): needs, job analysis, sourcing, screening, interviews, assessments, background checks, decision, offer, onboarding.
  • Selection (6): preliminary interview, application, references, tests, interview, decision.
  • Internal sources: promotion, transfer, demotion, retired employees, notice board. External: ads, institutes, placement and employment agencies, walk-ins, recommendations.
  • Tests: characteristics (physical, abilities, interests, personality); psychology (aptitude, achievement, situational, interest, personality, multi-dimensional).
  • T&D (5 steps): needs, design, delivery, evaluation, follow-up. Trends (6): digital, personalised, microlearning, gamification, DEI, soft skills.
  • OJT: apprenticeship, coaching, internship, job rotation. Off-the-job: conferences, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule, programmed instruction.
  • Systems approach: plans → managers required + inventory → analysis → sources → recruit/select/place/promote/separate → appraise, career, T&D → leading and controlling.
Chapter 5: Leading and controlling
  • Maslow: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation.
  • Herzberg: hygiene (salary, conditions, policy, supervision, relationships) vs motivators (achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth).
  • McGregor: X (control, autocratic) vs Y (trust, democratic).
  • Lewin: autocratic, democratic, free rein. Likert: 1 exploitative, 2 benevolent, 3 consultative, 4 participative. Grid: 1,1; 1,9; 9,1; 5,5; 9,9.
  • Group stages: forming, storming, norming, performing.
  • Communication: sender, encoding, transmission, reception, decoding, receiver, feedback; noise. 9 types.
  • Control (8): standards, actual performance, measure, compare, deviations, causes, corrective program, implement. Types: feed-forward, concurrent, feedback. Standards: physical, technical, monetary, managerial, time.
  • PERT: te = (o + 4m + p)/6.

Five golden habits for the exam

  1. Name it, quote the line, explain why in every case question.
  2. Draw the diagram whenever the question says “sketch”, “chart”, “diagram” or “representation”; label every box.
  3. Match the number of points to the marks: 3 marks ≈ three clear points with examples; 4 marks ≈ four.
  4. Use a real company example in every application question (Tata, Infosys, Maruti, Nestlé, Amazon, Reliance).
  5. Finish with a one-line conclusion that ties back to the question.
